Part 7: IT-01 Income Tax Computation Skeleton, Rates & Personal Allowance

Core pro-forma structure, column layout, ordering of income, and standard PA rules.

📐 Income Tax Pro-Forma Layout

Income tax is calculated using three dedicated columns in a strict left-to-right order:

Income Header Non-Savings (£) Savings (£) Dividend (£) Total (£)
Employment income / Trading profits / Pensions / Property X,XXX — — X,XXX
Bank & Building Society interest / Gilts interest — X,XXX — X,XXX
UK Dividend income — — X,XXX X,XXX
TOTAL INCOME X,XXX X,XXX X,XXX X,XXX
Less: Qualifying Interest Payments (X,XXX) — — (X,XXX)
NET INCOME X,XXX X,XXX X,XXX X,XXX
Less: Personal Allowance (£12,570 standard) (12,570) — — (12,570)
TAXABLE INCOME X,XXX X,XXX X,XXX X,XXX
🧠 MEMORY HOOK: ORDER OF DEDUCTIONS
Deduct allowable losses and Personal Allowance against income in the following order:
1️⃣ Non-Savings Income first (maximizes tax relief at 20%/40%/45%).
2️⃣ Savings Income second.
3️⃣ Dividend Income last (lowest tax rates: 8.75%/33.75%/39.35%).
⚠️ TRAP WARNING: PA DEDUCTION IN EXAMS
Never allocate Personal Allowance against dividend income if there is remaining non-savings or savings income. Always absorb non-savings income first!

Part 8: IT-02 Savings & Dividend Income Rules + Practice Drills

Starting rate band (0%), Nil Rate Bands (SNRB & DNRB), Gilt interest rules, and questions Q1, Q2, Q15–Q18.

📖 Core Rules: Savings & Dividends

1. Starting Rate for Savings (0% up to £5,000): Applies ONLY if taxable non-savings income is less than £5,000. Each £1 of taxable non-savings income reduces the starting rate band by £1.

2. Savings Nil Rate Band (SNRB): Basic rate taxpayer = £1,000 @ 0% | Higher rate taxpayer = £500 @ 0% | Additional rate taxpayer = £0.

3. Dividend Nil Rate Band (DNRB): £500 @ 0% for ALL taxpayers regardless of total income.

4. Nil Rate Band Ordering: Nil rate bands use up slice capacity in the tax band (Basic rate £37,700), even though taxed at 0%.

Q15 • David's Income Tax Liability
+10 XP Section A OTQ

David received the following income for the tax year 2025/26:

  • Property income: £21,150
  • Interest from UK Government securities (gilts): £2,400
  • Dividends: £450

What is David's total income tax liability for the tax year 2025/26?

Property income: £21,150 Gilts interest (Savings): £2,400 Dividends: £450 ------- Net income: £24,000 Less Personal Allowance: (£12,570) ------- Taxable income: £11,430 ======= Analysis of Tax Liability: Non-savings (£21,150 - £12,570): £8,580 × 20% = £1,716 Savings SNRB: £1,000 × 0% = £0 Savings excess: £1,400 × 20% = £280 Dividends DNRB: £450 × 0% = £0 ------ Total Tax Liability: £1,996
CORRECT ANSWER: A (£1,996)
David is a basic rate taxpayer, so he receives a £1,000 Savings Nil Rate Band (SNRB) and a £500 Dividend Nil Rate Band (DNRB).
Q16 • Harrison's Dividend Income Tax Liability
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Harrison's only income in the tax year 2025/26 was dividend income of £56,950. What is Harrison's income tax liability for the tax year 2025/26?

📋 EXAMINER TIP — Dividend Tax & PA Interaction (PDF p.260+ / Part 8)

Dividend tax applies after PA. If ANI > £100,000, PA is tapered — this affects dividend liability directly. Always check PA first, then apply dividend rates (8% / 33.75% / 39.35%) to amount above PA.

Common trap: Forgetting that pension contributions reduce PA restriction calculation (they do NOT reduce Class 4 NIC — separate rule).

Gross Dividend Income: £56,950 Less Personal Allowance: (£12,570) ------- Taxable Dividend Income: £44,380 Income Tax Liability: Dividend Nil Rate Band (£500 × 0%): £0 Basic Rate Band (£37,200 × 8.75%): £3,255 Higher Rate Band ((£44,380 - £37,700) = £6,680 × 33.75%): £2,255 ------ Total Income Tax Liability: £5,510
CORRECT ANSWER: £5,510
The dividend nil rate band is £500. It uses up part of the basic rate band (£37,700), leaving £37,200 taxed at basic rate (8.75%) and the remaining £6,680 taxed at higher rate (33.75%).
ACT 1 • INCOME TAX & NIC

Part 9: IT-03 Personal Allowance Restriction, Gift Aid & Marriage Allowance

Tapering over £100k, Adjusted Net Income (ANI) calculation, Qualifying Interest, and questions Q9, Q12, Q13, Q14.

📖 Core Rules: PA Restriction & Adjusted Net Income (ANI)

1. Adjusted Net Income Formula:

ANI = Net Income - Gross Gift Aid Donations - Gross Personal Pension Contributions

2. PA Taper Rule: Where ANI exceeds £100,000, Personal Allowance is reduced by £1 for every £2 of excess above £100,000.

3. Full Loss of PA: At ANI of £125,140 or more, Personal Allowance is reduced to £Nil (£12,570 / 0.5 = £25,140 excess).

4. Marriage Allowance Transfer: A spouse/civil partner with unutilised PA can transfer £1,260 to their partner, provided the recipient is a basic rate taxpayer. Gives a fixed tax reduction of £252 (£1,260 × 20%).

Q14 • Ines' Personal Allowance
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Ines is a sole trader. During the tax year 2025/26 she had taxable trading income of £106,800 and received dividend income of £1,500. Ines made a gift aid donation of £2,000 (gross) during the tax year 2025/26.

What amount of personal allowance is Ines entitled to for the tax year 2025/26?

Trading Income: £106,800 Dividend Income: £1,500 -------- Net Income: £108,300 Less: Gross Gift Aid: (£2,000) -------- Adjusted Net Income (ANI): £106,300 Less Income Limit: (£100,000) -------- Excess Income: £6,300 -------- PA Reduction (50% × £6,300): £3,150 Standard PA: £12,570 Less Reduction: (£3,150) -------- Entitled Personal Allowance: £9,420
CORRECT ANSWER: £9,420
Remember to deduct gross Gift Aid donations to arrive at Adjusted Net Income BEFORE applying the 50% taper threshold!
Q8 • Dane & Zara Property Splitting & Child Benefit (Kaplan Kit physical p.3)
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Dane and Zara are a married couple. They jointly own a residential letting property generating £20,000 letting profits. Dane owns 25% and Zara owns 75%. No election is made regarding income splitting. Zara earns employment income of £85,000, and Dane receives £2,252 of child benefit. Dane has no other income.

Which of the following statements are correct in relation to Zara's income tax liability for 2025/26?

Property splitting rules (Spouses): Without an election to specify actual shares, jointly owned property profits must be split 50:50. Zara's property share: 50% × £20,000 = £10,000. Zara's total income = £85,000 employment + £10,000 property = £95,000. Zara's taxable income = £95,000 - PA £12,570 = £82,430 (Taxable). Child Benefit Charge (HICBC): The HICBC threshold is £60,000 (ANI). Since Zara's adjusted net income (£95,000) exceeds £80,000, the charge is 100% of child benefit received = £2,252. Marriage Allowance: Transferable PA is only available if neither spouse is a higher-rate taxpayer. Zara earns £95,000 (higher rate), so no transfer is allowed. Joint Election Benefits: If they elected to split 25:75, Zara would be taxed on 75% (£15,000) at 40% tax rate. Without the election, she is taxed on 50% (£10,000) at 40%. Therefore, the election is NOT beneficial.
CORRECT ANSWER: A
Tutor's Tip: By default, spouses are taxed 50:50 on joint letting property unless they file Form 17 showing actual shares. In this case, 50:50 saves Zara money because she is in the higher bracket!
ACT 1 • INCOME TAX & NIC

Part 10: IT-04 Child Benefit Charge & Statutory Residence Test (SRT)

High Income Child Benefit Charge (£60k–£80k), SRT automatic tests, UK ties, and questions Q3–Q8, Q10, Q11.

📖 Core Rules: High Income Child Benefit Charge (HICBC)

1. Threshold: Applies to an individual whose Adjusted Net Income exceeds £60,000 where either they or their partner receive Child Benefit.

2. Charge Formula: The charge is 1% of the total Child Benefit received for every £200 of ANI between £60,000 and £80,000.

3. 100% Clawback: If ANI reaches £80,000 or more, the tax charge equals 100% of the Child Benefit received.

Q10 • Chi's Child Benefit Charge
+10 XP Section A OTQ

For the tax year 2025/26, Chi has a salary of £66,200. She received child benefit of £2,252 during this tax year.

What is Chi's child benefit income tax charge for the tax year 2025/26?

Child Benefit Received: £2,252 Salary (ANI): £66,200 Less Lower Limit: (£60,000) -------- Excess Income: £6,200 Percentage Charge: £6,200 / £200 = 31% Child Benefit Tax Charge: 31% × £2,252 = £698.12 -> Rounded down = £698
CORRECT ANSWER: £698
The tax charge is always rounded down to the nearest whole pound.

📖 Statutory Residence Test (SRT) Summary

1. Automatic Overseas Test (Not Resident):

  • In UK for under 16 days during tax year (if resident in 1+ of previous 3 years).
  • In UK for under 46 days during tax year (if not resident in any of previous 3 years).
  • Works full-time overseas and spends under 91 days in UK (and under 31 working days in UK).

2. Automatic UK Test (Resident):

  • In UK for 183 days or more in the tax year.
  • Only home is in the UK (available for 91+ consecutive days and occupied for 30+ days).
  • Works full-time in the UK.
ACT 1 • INCOME TAX & NIC

Part 11: IT-05 Employment Income: Receipts Basis, Bonuses & Exempt Benefits

Rules of taxability, receipts basis timing, statutory exempt benefits, and practice questions Q32 & Q33.

📖 Core Rules: Receipts Basis & Timing of Bonuses

Employment income is taxed on the receipts basis. For directors and employees, earnings are treated as received on the earliest of:

  • 1. The date payment is actually received.
  • 2. The date the person becomes entitled to payment.
  • 3. (For directors) The date earnings are credited in the company's accounts or end of period of account.
⚠️ TRAP WARNING: BONUS TIMING
A bonus voted in respect of a calendar year (e.g. year to 31 Dec 2024) but paid on 6 April 2025 falls into the tax year 2025/26 because it was received/entitled on 6 April 2025!

🎁 Statutory Exempt Benefits Master List

The following employee benefits are 100% exempt from Income Tax and Class 1A NIC:

Exempt BenefitStatutory Condition / Limits
Workplace ParkingParking spaces at or near the employee's place of work.
Subscribed Professional FeesSubscriptions to HMRC-approved professional bodies (e.g. ACCA, CIM).
Workplace Canteen / MealsAvailable to ALL employees on a non-discriminatory basis.
Job-Related Relocation ExpensesUp to £8,000 max per move.
Work Mobile PhoneOne mobile phone provided per employee (including line rental and calls).
Annual Parties / EventsUp to £150 per head per year (inclusive of VAT).
Trivial BenefitsCost under £50 per gift, not cash or cash equivalent.

🚗 Company Car & Fuel Benefit Formulas (FA2025)

Car Benefit = List Price × Appropriate Percentage (%) Fuel Benefit = £28,200 × Appropriate Percentage (%)
Vehicle CO₂ BandAppropriate % (Petrol & RDE2 Diesel)
0g/km (Pure Electric)3%

⚠️ TRAP WARNING: DIESEL SURCHARGE
Diesel cars NOT meeting the RDE2 standard suffer a 4% surcharge (capped at 37%). If the question states the diesel car meets RDE2 standard, do NOT add 4%!

🚚 Van Benefits, Accommodation & Beneficial Loans

• Company Van Benefit: Flat charge of £4,020 (Zero emission vans = £0 benefit). Fuel scale charge = £769.

• Beneficial Loans: Taxable if loan exceeds £10,000 at any point in the tax year. Benefit = Loan × (Official Interest Rate 3.75% - Interest Paid).

• Approved Mileage Allowance Payments (AMAP): Cars/Vans: 45p/mile for first 10,000 business miles; 25p/mile over 10,000 miles.

Q27 • Thiago's Company Car Benefit
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Thiago is provided with a new diesel company car on 6 May 2025 (used for business and private purposes). List price is £28,000, CO₂ emissions 152g/km, meets RDE2 standard.

What is Thiago's car benefit for the tax year 2025/26?

List Price: £28,000 CO2 emissions: 152g/km Base level 55g/km = 17% (152 - 55) = 97g/km / 5 = 19.4 -> 19 steps of 5g/km × 1% = +19% Base percentage: 17% + 19% = 36% RDE2 standard diesel -> NO 4% surcharge! Full Year Benefit: £28,000 × 36% = £10,080 Provided from 6 May 2025 -> 11 months in tax year 2025/26 (May to March + April = 11 months): 11/12 × £10,080 = £9,240
CORRECT ANSWER: £9,240
Remember to time-apportion benefits when provided part-way through the tax year (6 May = 11 months)!

Q41 • Ronald's Cessation Capital Allowances
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Ronald ceased trading on 31 March 2026. Main pool TWDV at 1 April 2025 = £15,000. On 1 Jan 2026 bought business laptop for £4,500. On 31 March 2026 main pool items sold for £14,550. Laptop retained by Ronald (market value £4,150).

What is the capital allowance / (balancing charge) for the year ended 31 March 2026?

TWDV b/fwd 1 April 2025: £15,000 Add: Laptop purchase: £4,500 -------- Subtotal: £19,500 Disposals on Cessation: - Main pool items sold: (£14,550) - Laptop retained (MV): (£4,150) -------- Remaining Unrelieved Balance: £800 Balancing Allowance on Cessation = £800
CORRECT ANSWER: D (£800 Balancing Allowance)
On cessation, NO WDA or AIA is claimed. Instead, compare total pool value against total disposal proceeds/market values to arrive at a Balancing Allowance (+£800) or Balancing Charge.

Q47 • Naomi's Loss Relief Cap
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Naomi made a trading loss of £110,000 in 2025/26. In 2024/25 she had trading profit of £24,000 and employment income of £92,000 (Total income = £116,000).

What is the maximum loss relief claim Naomi can make against her total income for 2024/25?

Total Income 2024/25: £24,000 + £92,000 = £116,000 Statutory Cap on Non-Trading Income Set-Off: Higher of £50,000 or 25% × Total Income (25% × £116,000 = £29,000) Statutory Cap = £50,000 HOWEVER: Cap applies ONLY to non-trading income (£92,000)! Trading profit (£24,000) can be FULLY relieved without cap! Max Claim = Trading Profit (£24,000) + Cap on Non-Trading Income (£50,000) Max Claim = £24,000 + £50,000 = £74,000
CORRECT ANSWER: A (£74,000)
Classic examiner trap! The £50k cap applies ONLY to non-trading income. Trading income within total income is relieved 100% cap-free!

Part 16: IT-10 Partnership Taxation

🤝 Partnership Profit Allocation Rules

1. Partnership trading profit is calculated at the partnership level using standard sole trader tax adjustment rules.

2. Profits are allocated among partners in accordance with the profit-sharing agreement for that accounting period:

Step 1: Allocate partner salaries (pro-rata for period). Step 2: Allocate partner interest on capital. Step 3: Divide remaining balance in Profit Sharing Ratio (PSR).
Q44 • Elizabeth & Henry Partnership Allocation
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Elizabeth and Henry share profits to 31 Dec 2025 (£120,000 total profit). Until 31 July 2025 ratio was 70:30 (no salaries). From 1 August 2025 ratio was 80:20 after Henry salary of £24,000 p.a.

How much profit for year ended 31 Dec 2025 is allocated to Henry?

Period 1: 1 Jan 2025 - 31 July 2025 (7 months): Profit = 7/12 × £120,000 = £70,000 Henry's Share (30%) = £21,000 Period 2: 1 Aug 2025 - 31 Dec 2025 (5 months): Profit = 5/12 × £120,000 = £50,000 Henry's Salary = 5/12 × £24,000 = £10,000 Remaining Profit = £50,000 - £10,000 = £40,000 Henry's Share (20%) = £8,000 Total Henry Period 2 = £10,000 + £8,000 = £18,000 Total Allocation to Henry = £21,000 + £18,000 = £39,000
CORRECT ANSWER: D (£39,000)
Always split the accounting year into sub-periods whenever PSR or salaries change!

Part 18: IT-12 Pension Reliefs & Annual Allowance Charge

Occupational vs Personal Pensions, Annual Allowance (£60,000), Tapered Annual Allowance, carry-forward rules, and Q64–Q69.

🏦 Pension Relief & Annual Allowance Rules

1. Personal Pension Relief: Taxpayer pays 80% net; pension provider claims 20% basic rate relief at source. Basic and higher rate tax bands are extended by the GROSS contribution.

2. Annual Allowance (AA): Standard Annual Allowance is £60,000 per tax year.

3. Carry-Forward Unused AA: Unused AA from the preceding 3 tax years can be brought forward, provided the taxpayer was a member of a registered pension scheme in those years (used on a FIFO basis).

4. Tapered Annual Allowance: Applies if Adjusted Income exceeds £260,000 AND Threshold Income exceeds £200,000. Reduced by £1 for every £2 over £260,000 (Minimum tapered AA = £10,000).

Q66 • Abena's Pension Contribution
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Abena made gross personal pension contributions: 2022/23 £42k, 2023/24 £57k, 2024/25 £48k. (AA was £40k in 2022/23, £60k in 2023/24 and 2024/25).

What is the maximum gross contribution Abena can make in 2025/26 without giving rise to an AA charge?

2025/26 Current Year AA: £60,000 Brought Forward Unused AA: - 2022/23 (£40,000 - £42,000): £0 (Fully used) - 2023/24 (£60,000 - £57,000): £3,000 - 2024/25 (£60,000 - £48,000): £12,000 ------- Total Capacity 2025/26 = £60k + £3k + £12k = £75,000
CORRECT ANSWER: C (£75,000)
Current year AA is always used first, then brought-forward unused allowances on a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) basis.

Payments on account are NOT required if either:

Payments on account are based ALWAYS on 50% of the PRECEDING year's net tax liability after deducting PAYE/source tax!

Q13 • Ifram's Qualifying Interest Payments
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Loan Interest DescriptionQualifyingNot Qualifying
Loan to purchase a laptop for employment use[ ][ ]
Mortgage on main private residence[ ][ ]

Q19 • Nicolas' Office Lease Premium
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Nicolas granted a 15-year lease on an unfurnished freehold office building on 6 April 2025 for a premium of £82,000. How much is taxable as property income for 2025/26?

Capital Premium Received: £82,000 Lease Term (N): 15 years Property Income Taxable Portion: £82,000 × [51 - (15 - 1)] / 50 = £82,000 × (51 - 14) / 50 = £82,000 × 37 / 50 = £60,680... wait! Let's check 51 - 14 = 37 / 50 = 74% × £82,000 = £60,680 (or £59,040 if N=15: £82,000 × 51 - 15 = 36/50 = 72% × £82,000 = £59,040).
CORRECT ANSWER: A (£59,040)
Taxable property income = Premium × [51 - (N - 1)] / 50 = £82,000 × [51 - 15] / 50 = £82,000 × 36/50 = £59,040.

Q50 • Sabine's Opening Years Loss
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Sabine started trading 1 April 2024. Year to 31 March 2025 profit = £5,000; Year to 31 March 2026 loss = (£25,000). Employed until 31 March 2024 (£45,000 p.a.). Receives £3,000 savings income p.a. What is the EARLIEST tax year in which her loss can be offset?

Loss incurred in 2025/26 (tax year 2 of trade). Under s.72 Opening Years Loss Relief: Loss incurred in first 4 tax years of trade can be carried back 3 tax years on FIFO basis! First tax year of trade = 2023/24 (1 April 2024 falls in 2023/24). Loss year = 2025/26. Carry back 3 years before 2025/26: 1st year FIFO = 2022/23! Income in 2022/23 = Employment Income (£45,000) + Savings (£3,000) = £48,000. Sabine can relieve the FULL £25,000 loss against 2022/23 income!
CORRECT ANSWER: Earliest Tax Year = 2022/23 | Loss Relieved = £25,000
Opening years loss relief (s.72) allows a 3-year carry-back on a First-In, First-Out (FIFO) basis against total income!

Adjusted Income: £330,000 Threshold Limit: £260,000 Excess Adjusted Income = £330,000 - £260,000 = £70,000 Taper Reduction = 50% × £70,000 = £35,000 Tapered Annual Allowance = Standard AA (£60,000) - £35,000 = £25,000 Pension Contribution Made: £100,000 Less Tapered AA Available: (£25,000) -------- Annual Allowance Chargeable Amount = £75,000

🛡️ Professional Conduct in Relation to Taxation (PCRT)

1. Five Fundamental Principles: Integrity, Objectivity, Professional Competence & Due Care, Confidentiality, Professional Behavior.

2. Tax Evasion vs Avoidance: Evasion is ILLEGAL (deliberate suppression of facts). Avoidance is LEGAL structuring within the spirit/letter of the law.

3. Money Laundering Regulations (MLR): Advisers MUST disclose suspicious transactions to the Money Laundering Reporting Officer (MLRO) or National Crime Agency (NCA). Tipping off the client is a criminal offense!

Q93 • Philip and Charles (10 Marks)

Scenario: Philip retired at 55. Received pension £15,000 and building society interest £14,600 in 2025/26. Charles (son) is self-employed (trading profit £112,400). Charles made Gift Aid £800 (gross) and gross pension contribution £45,000 in 2023/24 (none since).

CORRECT ANSWER: C (£3,206)

⚠️ TRAP WARNING: ALLOCATION OF AEA (£3,000)
Always allocate the Annual Exempt Amount (£3,000) against gains taxed at the HIGHEST rate first (e.g. 24% gains before BADR 14% gains) to minimize tax liability!

Part 41: CGT-02 Chattels, Wasting Assets & Part Disposals

Tangible moveable property, £6,000 gross rule, 5/3rds marginal gain cap, and the part disposal formula A / (A + B).

🖼️ Chattels Tax Rules Matrix

Cost / Proceeds CategoryGross Proceeds ≤ £6,000Gross Proceeds > £6,000
Cost ≤ £6,000EXEMPT from CGTGain capped at 5/3 × (Gross Proceeds - £6,000)
Cost > £6,000Deemed Gross Proceeds = £6,000 (Limits loss)Normal CGT Computation (Proceeds - Cost)
⚠️ TRAP WARNING: WASTING CHATTELS
Wasting chattels (predictable useful life ≤ 50 years, e.g. racehorses, private motor cars, greyhounds, plant & machinery) are 100% EXEMPT from CGT, provided they are not used in a trade eligible for capital allowances!

📐 Part Disposal Cost Allocation Formula

Where part of an asset is sold, allowable cost is calculated as:

Allowable Cost = Original Total Cost × [ A / (A + B) ] Where: A = Gross proceeds of part sold B = Market value of remaining unsold portion

Part 42: CGT-03 Shares Matching Rules, Takeovers & Spousal Transfers

Individual share matching hierarchy, bonus/rights issues, Section 104 Share Pool, and no gain/no loss spousal transfers.

📈 Individual Share Matching Hierarchy

Disposals of shares by individuals are matched against acquisitions in the following strict priority:

1. Same day acquisitions (Shares acquired on the exact day of disposal). 2. Next 30 days acquisitions (Shares acquired within 30 days AFTER disposal, FIFO). 3. Section 104 Share Pool (Averaged pool of all remaining shares).

👩‍❤️‍👨 Spousal Transfer Rule

Transfers of assets between spouses / civil partners living together take place on a no gain / no loss basis. Deemed proceeds = Transferor's allowable cost (no taxable gain or loss arises).

🏡 Principal Private Residence Relief (PRR)

PRR Exempt Gain = Total Chargeable Gain × [ Period of Deemed / Actual Occupation / Total Ownership Period ] Deemed Occupation Periods (Provided house was occupied BEFORE and AFTER): 1. Final 9 months of ownership (ALWAYS EXEMPT regardless of actual occupation). 2. Up to 3 years of absence for ANY reason. 3. Unlimited absence while working ABROAD. 4. Up to 4 years of absence while working elsewhere in the UK.

Part 44: CGT-05 Corporate Chargeable Gains & Indexation Allowance

Indexation allowance frozen at December 2017, company share pool structure, and Corporation Tax rate application.

🏛️ Corporate Gains vs Individual CGT Rules

1. No AEA for Companies: Companies do NOT receive the £3,000 Annual Exempt Amount.

2. Indexation Allowance (IA): Companies receive Indexation Allowance to deduct inflation. Indexation was frozen at December 2017 (no indexation allowed for inflation after Dec 2017).

3. Indexation Cannot Create or Increase a Loss: IA can only reduce a gain to £Nil.

Q141 • Lotte's Destroyed Warehouse Reinvestment
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Lotte bought warehouse for £52,000 in Nov 2020. Destroyed by fire June 2025. Insurance proceeds received = £71,000. Reinvested £64,000 in new warehouse. Lotte claims maximum deferral. What is the base cost of the new warehouse?

Full Insurance Proceeds: £71,000 Cost of Destroyed Warehouse: (£52,000) -------- Full Chargeable Gain: £19,000 Proceeds NOT reinvested: £71,000 - £64,000 = £7,000 (Taxable immediately!) Gain Deferred = Full Gain (£19,000) - Immediate Gain (£7,000) = £12,000 Base Cost of New Warehouse: New Purchase Price (£64,000) - Deferred Gain (£12,000) = £52,000
CORRECT ANSWER: B (£52,000)
Where partial reinvestment occurs under s.23 insurance relief, gain deferred = full gain minus un-reinvested proceeds (£19k - £7k = £12k). Base cost = £64k - £12k = £52k.

Part 54: IHT-01 Lifetime Transfers, Exemptions & PET vs CLT Classification

Potentially Exempt Transfers (PETs), Chargeable Lifetime Transfers (CLTs), Annual Exemption (£3,000), Small Gifts (£250), Marriage gifts, and spouse transfers.

🏛️ Classification of Lifetime Gifts Matrix

Recipient / Gift TypeIHT ClassificationImmediate Lifetime Tax?
Spouse / Civil Partner100% EXEMPT TransferNO (0% tax)
Individual (e.g. Son / Daughter / Friend)Potentially Exempt Transfer (PET)NO (Taxable ONLY if donor dies within 7 years)
Discretionary Trust / CompanyChargeable Lifetime Transfer (CLT)YES (Immediate lifetime tax @ 20% or 25%)

🎁 Master List of Statutory IHT Exemptions

1. Spouse Exemption: Unlimited transfers between UK-domiciled spouses.

2. Annual Exemption (AE): £3,000 per tax year. Unused AE can be carried forward 1 tax year only (used AFTER current year AE).

3. Small Gifts Exemption: Up to £250 per recipient per tax year (cannot be combined with AE on same person).

4. Marriage / Civil Partnership Exemption: Parent = £5,000 | Grandparent / Remote ancestor = £2,500 | Bride / Groom to each other = £2,500 | Any other person = £1,000.

5. Normal Expenditure Out of Income: Exempt if paid regularly out of surplus net income without reducing standard of living.

Part 55: IHT-02 Lifetime Tax Computations, Cumulation & Death Taper Relief

Grossing up rules (20% donee vs 25% donor), 7-year cumulation window, Nil Rate Band (£325k), and Taper Relief table.

📊 Death Taper Relief Table (Gifts Made 3–7 Years Prior to Death)

Years Between Gift and DeathPercentage Reduction in TaxEffective Tax Rate on Excess
0 to 3 years0% (No reduction)40.0%
More than 3 but less than 4 years20% reduction32.0%
More than 4 but less than 5 years40% reduction24.0%
More than 5 but less than 6 years60% reduction16.0%
More than 6 but less than 7 years80% reduction8.0%
7 years or more100% EXEMPT0.0%
⚠️ TRAP WARNING: TAPER RELIEF APPLIES TO TAX, NOT GIFT VALUE
Taper relief reduces the INHERITANCE TAX PAYABLE, NOT the value of the gift! Always calculate full tax at 40% on excess over NRB first, then apply the taper % reduction!

Part 56: IHT-03 Death Estate Computation, NRB, RNRB & Spouse Transfers

Nil Rate Band (£325,000), Residence Nil Rate Band (£175,000), unutilised spouse NRB/RNRB transfer (up to 100%), and 40% death tax rate.

🏠 Residence Nil Rate Band (RNRB) Rules

1. RNRB Maximum: £175,000 per individual (FA2025).

2. Qualifying Criteria: Applies when a main residence is left to direct descendants (children, step-children, grandchildren).

3. Unused RNRB Spouse Transfer: Up to 100% of unused RNRB can be transferred to a surviving spouse (providing a total potential combined tax-free threshold of £1,000,000 = £325k + £325k NRB + £175k + £175k RNRB!).

4. RNRB Taper Threshold: Tapered by £1 for every £2 that the gross death estate exceeds £2,000,000.

Part 58: Section A IHT Practice Drills (Q180–Q190)

Lifetime exemptions, PET death tax, taper relief, and grossing up.

Q181 • Cora's Death Tax on PET
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Cora gave cash £300,000 to niece on 30 April 2020. Made cash gift £500,000 to nephew on 31 May 2021 (after deducting exemptions). Cora died on 31 October 2025. What IHT was payable on death in respect of the £500,000 gift to her nephew?

Gift 1 (30 April 2020): £300,000 PET -> Uses £300,000 of NRB (£325,000). Remaining NRB available for Gift 2 = £325,000 - £300,000 = £25,000. Gift 2 (31 May 2021): £500,000 PET to nephew. Less Remaining NRB: (£25,000) -------- Excess Taxable Amount: £475,000 Full Death Tax @ 40%: £475,000 × 40% = £190,000 Taper Relief Check: Gift date 31 May 2021 -> Death 31 Oct 2025. Time elapsed = 4 years and 5 months (More than 4 but less than 5 years). Taper Relief = 40% reduction! Tax Payable = £190,000 × (100% - 40%) = £190,000 × 60% = £114,000
CORRECT ANSWER: C (£114,000)
Remember 7-year cumulation absorbs NRB in order of gifts made, and taper relief reduces full 40% tax by 40% for gifts made 4-5 years prior to death!

Q195 • Dominic's Unquoted Share Valuation
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Dominic owned 7,500 shares (75%) in Halder Ltd. On 1 July 2025 gave 3,000 shares to his son (retaining 4,500 shares = 45%). Share values: up to 25% @ £5/sh, 26-50% @ £8/sh, 51-74% @ £13/sh, 75%+ @ £20/sh. What is the transfer of value for IHT?

Loss to Donor Principle: Value of holding BEFORE gift (7,500 shares = 75% holding): 7,500 shares × £20 per share = £150,000 Value of holding AFTER gift (4,500 shares = 45% holding): 4,500 shares × £8 per share = (£36,000) --------- Transfer of Value (Loss to Donor) = £114,000
CORRECT ANSWER: £114,000
Lifetime IHT value is calculated strictly on the "Loss to Donor" principle (Value before gift minus Value after gift), NOT on the value received by the donee!

Part 64: CT-01 Corporation Tax Accounting Periods, FY2023–2025 Rates & Marginal Relief

Accounting periods (max 12 months), Small Profits Rate (19%), Main Rate (25%), Marginal Relief formula (3/200ths), and Associated Companies division.

🏢 Corporation Tax Rates & Thresholds (FA2025)

Profits Level (Augmented Profits)Tax Rate / Tax TreatmentUpper / Lower Threshold (Divided by N)
Profits ≤ £50,000 / NSmall Profits Rate = 19%Lower Limit = £50,000 / N
£50,000 / N < Profits ≤ £250,000 / NMain Rate 25% LESS Marginal ReliefMarginal Relief Zone
Profits > £250,000 / NMain Rate = 25%Upper Limit = £250,000 / N
Marginal Relief Formula = (3 / 200) × [ Upper Limit - Augmented Profits ] × ( Taxable Total Profits / Augmented Profits ) Where: • N = 1 + Number of Associated Companies worldwide. • Augmented Profits = Taxable Total Profits (TTP) + Exempt ABGH Dividends from non-group companies.
⚠️ TRAP WARNING: ASSOCIATED COMPANIES DIVISION
Upper (£250k) and Lower (£50k) limits are divided by N (where N = the company ITSELF + all worldwide associated companies active at any point in the AP). Do NOT count dormant companies!

Part 65: CT-02 Trading Adjustments, Non-Trade Loan Relationships (NTLR) & Property Income

Disallowable items for companies, NTLR interest received vs non-trade interest paid, and Qualifying Charitable Donations (QCD).

📖 Non-Trade Loan Relationships (NTLR) Rules

NTLR Net Income = Non-Trading Interest Received (Accruals basis) - Non-Trading Interest Paid (Accruals basis) • Interest paid on trading loans (e.g. loan to purchase delivery vans) = ALLOWABLE TRADING EXPENSE. • Interest paid on non-trading loans (e.g. loan to buy shares / investment property) = DEDUCTED IN NTLR.

Part 66: CT-03 Corporate Capital Allowances: Full Expensing & 50% Special Rate FYA

Full Expensing (100% FYA on main pool new plant & machinery), 50% Special Rate Pool FYA, AIA (£1M), and Structures & Buildings Allowance (SBA 3%).

⚙️ Corporate Capital Allowances Matrix (FA2025)

Allowance TypeRate & Pool AllocationQualifying Assets
Full Expensing (100% FYA)100% FYA (No cap limit!)NEW & unused main pool plant & machinery purchased by companies.
50% Special Rate FYA50% FYA (Balance to SR Pool @ 6%)NEW & unused special rate pool assets (integral features).
Annual Investment Allowance (AIA)100% FYA (Limit £1,000,000 p.a.)Used or new assets, cars EXCLUDED.
Structures & Buildings Allowance (SBA)3% Straight Line p.a.New commercial structures/buildings.
🧠 MEMORY HOOK: FULL EXPENSING VS AIA ALLOCATION
Always allocate Full Expensing (100% FYA) to NEW main pool assets first. Then use AIA (£1,000,000) on SPECIAL RATE POOL assets (to get 100% immediate relief instead of 50% FYA)!

Q218 • Flower Ltd's NTLR Income
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Flower Ltd's year ended 31 March 2026 results: Loan interest rec'd £35,000 (accrued £5,000). Loan interest paid on van fleet £10,000; Loan interest paid on loan to buy shares in trading company £8,000. What is NTLR income included in TTP?

Non-Trading Interest Receivable (Accruals basis): Received £35,000 + Accrued £5,000 = £40,000 Non-Trading Interest Payable: • Interest on van fleet loan (£10,000) = TRADING EXPENSE (Deductible in trade profit). • Interest on share acquisition loan (£8,000) = NON-TRADE LOAN RELATIONSHIP DEDUCTION. NTLR Net Income = £40,000 - £8,000 = £32,000
CORRECT ANSWER: £32,000
Remember trade loan interest is a trading deduction, while non-trade interest paid is offset against non-trade interest received in NTLR!

Q224 • Edam Ltd's Capital Allowances
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Edam Ltd (VAT registered) bought a second-hand lorry for £198,000 (inc VAT £33,000) during year ended 31 March 2026. Main pool TWDV b/fwd at 1 April 2025 was £15,000. What is maximum capital allowance Edam Ltd can claim?

Lorry Cost (Net of VAT for VAT-registered company): £198,000 - £33,000 = £165,000 Note: Second-hand lorry does NOT qualify for Full Expensing (100% FYA applies to NEW assets only!). However, second-hand lorry QUALIFIES for Annual Investment Allowance (AIA)! AIA Claimed = £165,000 (100% within £1M limit) Main Pool WDA: TWDV b/fwd £15,000 × 18% WDA = £2,700 Total Capital Allowances = £165,000 (AIA) + £2,700 (WDA) = £167,700
CORRECT ANSWER: A (£167,700)
VAT-registered companies claim capital allowances on net-of-VAT cost. Second-hand assets do not qualify for Full Expensing but receive 100% AIA!

Part 72: Section A CT Practice Drills (Q233–Q242)

Group relief loss surrenders, gains group transfers, and 75% group relationships.

Q236 • Ten Ltd's Group Relationships
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Ten Ltd owns 90% of Twenty Ltd; Twenty Ltd owns 75% of Thirty Ltd; Thirty Ltd owns 70% of Forty Ltd. What is the group relationship between Forty Ltd and Ten Ltd?

Group Relief Indirect Holding Check: Ten Ltd -> Twenty Ltd (90%) -> Thirty Ltd (75%) -> Forty Ltd (70%). Indirect Holding in Forty Ltd = 90% × 75% × 70% = 47.25% (< 75% required!). So Forty Ltd is NOT in Ten Ltd's Group Relief group! Chargeable Gains Group Check: Requires 75% DIRECT holding at each tier AND > 50% overall effective indirect holding. Thirty Ltd owns 70% of Forty Ltd (< 75% direct holding at bottom tier!). So Forty Ltd is NOT in Ten Ltd's Gains group either!
CORRECT ANSWER: D (Do not form a group for either purpose)
Group relief requires ≥ 75% indirect shareholding (47.25% fails). Gains group requires ≥ 75% direct shareholding at every link in the chain (70% fails).

Part 73: Section A CT Practice Drills (Q243–Q251)

Associated companies count, quarterly instalment thresholds, and filing penalties.

Q249 • Asher, Barton & Chelfry Quarterly Instalments
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Which of the three companies (Asher Ltd: TTP £700k, 3 associated; Barton Ltd: TTP £600k 4m AP, 0 associated; Chelfry Ltd: TTP £1.6M, 0 associated) will NOT have to pay CT by quarterly instalments?

Large Company Threshold = £1,500,000 / N Asher Ltd: N = 1 + 3 = 4. Threshold = £1,500,000 / 4 = £375,000. TTP £700,000 > £375,000 -> Asher Ltd IS Large (Pays Instalments!). Barton Ltd: 4-month AP. Threshold = £1,500,000 × 4/12 = £500,000. TTP £600,000 > £500,000 -> Barton Ltd IS Large (Pays Instalments!). Chelfry Ltd: N = 1. Threshold = £1,500,000. Previous TTP = £1,400,000 (< £1,500,000). Grace Period Exception: A company is NOT large if TTP < £10M AND it was NOT large in the preceding 12 months! Chelfry Ltd qualifies for the grace period exception!
CORRECT ANSWER: C (Chelfry Ltd)
Chelfry Ltd does NOT have to pay by instalments due to the 1-year grace period exception (it was not large in the preceding year and TTP < £10M)!

Part 81: VAT-01 Compulsory/Voluntary Registration & Tax Point Rules

Historic test (£90,000 threshold in 12m), Future test (£90,000 in next 30 days), Deregistration (£88,000), Basic vs Actual tax point (14-day rule), and pre-registration input VAT.

📊 VAT Registration & Deregistration Thresholds (FA2025)

Registration TestStatutory ThresholdNotification DeadlineEffective Registration Date
Historic TestTaxable supplies > £90,000 in past 12 monthsWithin 30 days of end of month threshold exceeded1st day of second month following threshold month
Future TestTaxable supplies > £90,000 in next 30 days aloneBy end of the 30-day periodBeginning of the 30-day period
Compulsory DeregistrationTaxable supplies ≤ £88,000 expected in next 12mNotify within 30 days of cessationDate of cessation / request

⏰ Basic vs Actual Tax Point Rules (14-Day Rule)

• Basic Tax Point = Date goods are removed/made available OR service completed. • Actual Tax Point Exceptions: 1. If payment received or VAT invoice issued BEFORE basic tax point -> Tax point = Date of payment / invoice. 2. If VAT invoice issued within 14 DAYS AFTER basic tax point -> Tax point = Date of invoice!
🟢 PRE-REGISTRATION INPUT VAT RECOVERY
A newly registered trader can reclaim pre-registration input VAT on:
• Goods: Incurred within 4 years prior to registration (provided goods are still held at registration date).
• Services: Incurred within 6 months prior to registration.
ACT 5 • VALUE ADDED TAX

Part 82: VAT-02 Output & Input VAT, Fuel Scale Charges & Impaired Debts

Standard rate 20%, non-recoverable input VAT (business entertainment, cars with private use), fuel scale charges, and bad debt relief.

🚘 Fuel Scale Charges & Bad Debt Relief Rules

1. Car Fuel Scale Charge: If an employer provides free fuel for private motoring in a company car and reclaims full input VAT on fuel, employer MUST account for output VAT on the quarterly scale charge.

2. Bad Debt Relief (Impaired Debts): Reclaim output VAT paid on bad debts if:

  • Debt is written off in business accounts.
  • Debt is over 6 months overdue from payment due date (or supply date if later).
  • Claim made within 4 years of becoming eligible.
ACT 5 • VALUE ADDED TAX

Part 83: VAT-03 Special VAT Schemes & MTD Penalty System

Cash Accounting (£1.35M / £1.6M limit), Annual Accounting (£1.35M / £1.6M limit), Flat Rate Scheme (£150k / £230k limit, 1% discount), and MTD penalty points system.

⚡ Special VAT Schemes Master Summary

Part 84: VAT-04 Overseas VAT, Reverse Charge, VAT Groups & TOGC

Import VAT vs reverse charge on overseas services, Transfer of Going Concern (TOGC) no supply rule, and VAT groups.

🌐 Overseas Services & Reverse Charge Mechanism

1. Reverse Charge on Imported Services: When a UK business receives services from an overseas supplier, the UK business accounts for BOTH output VAT and input VAT on its own VAT return (net £0 effect for fully taxable business!).

2. Transfer of Going Concern (TOGC): The sale of a business as a going concern is treated as NEITHER a supply of goods NOR a supply of services (0% VAT charged), provided the buyer carries on the same trade and is VAT registered.

Q276 • Yui's Pre-Registration Input VAT
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Yui started trading 1 April 2025, registered for VAT from 1 Jan 2026. Incurred input VAT of £110/month on hire of office equipment from 1 April 2025. How much input VAT can Yui reclaim on her first VAT return for quarter ended 31 March 2026?

Office Equipment Hire = SERVICE! Pre-registration limit for SERVICES = 6 months prior to registration date (1 Jan 2026)! Period eligible prior to registration: 1 July 2025 to 31 Dec 2025 = 6 months. Pre-registration input VAT = 6 months × £110 = £660. Current Quarter (1 Jan 2026 - 31 March 2026): 3 months × £110 = £330. Total Input VAT Reclaimable = £660 (pre-reg) + £330 (current) = £990
CORRECT ANSWER: B (£990)
Reclaim pre-registration service input VAT incurred in the 6 months prior to registration (£660) PLUS current quarter input VAT (£330) = £990!

Q290 • Hamza's Flat Rate Scheme Liability
+10 XP Section A OTQ

Hamza uses Flat Rate Scheme (11%). Net sales: £100,000 standard rated, £30,000 zero rated. Net purchases: £15,000. What is Hamza's VAT liability for year ended 31 March 2026?

Under Flat Rate Scheme: Gross VAT-inclusive turnover = Standard rated sales (inc 20% VAT) + Zero rated sales Standard rated gross = £100,000 × 1.20 = £120,000 Zero rated gross = £30,000 Total Gross Turnover = £120,000 + £30,000 = £150,000 FRS VAT Liability = £150,000 × 11% = £16,500
CORRECT ANSWER: B (£16,500)
Flat rate scheme percentage applies to total gross VAT-INCLUSIVE turnover (including zero-rated supplies)!

He was employed by Initial plc as a sales manager, but was considering resigning on 14 March 2025 and taking up an offer of employment with Subsequent plc which would commence on 15 March 2025. If employed by Subsequent plc, Jason would receive a higher base salary and more benefits compared to remaining employed by Initial plc. However, Jason wanted to know how much more income tax he would have to pay should he take up the new offer of employment. Part (a) for 2 marks required candidates to state one advantage and one disadvantage for an employee if their employer payrolled the taxabl e benefits provided to the employee. This section was not particularly well answered. Rather than just being asked to explain payro lling of benefits, candidates are also expected to know the advantages and disadvantages if an employer payrolls the taxable benefits provided to an employee. For example, an advantage to the employee could be either: • There is no need to declare payrolled benefits on the employee’s self-assessment tax return, or • The employee will not have any unexpected tax liabilities in respect of the taxable benefits which have been payrolled. And a disadvantage would be: • The tax due on the benefit will generally be paid earlier than if collected under self- assessment. Part (b) for 11 marks required a calculation of how much more income tax Jason would have had to pay for the tax year 2025/26 if he took up the offer of employment with Subsequent plc rather than remaining employed by Initial plc. This section was reasonably well answered. • Candidates should simply list any exempt items within the main computation and indicate as such by the use of zero (0) – not by an explanation. • Even though there might only be a ½ mark fo r recognising an exemption, it is important to know the various exemptions so that time is not spent in producing more complicated workings. • Candidates should note that many of the workings for this style of question can be included within the main computation. For example, the beneficial loan working (£140,000 × 3.75% × 8/12 = £3,500). The only aspect which warranted a separate working here was the living accommodation additional benefit. • With computations containing both additions and deductions, candidates should be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions included as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. • Jason was clearly an additional rate taxpayer under both employment alternatives, so the extra amount of income tax payable was simply the difference between the two amounts of employment income multiplied by the rate of 45%. Producing two income tax workings not only used more time, but meant that a mistake was much more likely. Practice as many computations as possible. If this is done, straightforward workings for the main benefits should become second nature, meaning that marks can be obtained quite quickly without making any basic mistakes. --- PAGE 310 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 264 KAPLAN PUBLISHING Part (c) for 2 marks required candidates (if Jason decided to resign as an employee of Initial plc) to explain the main content and purpose of PAYE form P45. This section was not particularly well answered. If a requirement is just for two marks, then just a few brief points are required in an answer. Of course, it is also important to know the difference between the different PAYE forms. The following answer would have been sufficient: • Form P45 will have shown Jason’s taxable earnings and income tax deducted up to the date of leaving, together with the tax code at this date. • Jason will have given a copy of the form to Subsequent plc so that they can correctly calculate PAYE for the remainder of 2024/25. 99 POPPY Key answer tips This section C question covers employment income, the accrued income scheme, partnerships and administration. Part (a) offers some easy marks for calculating basic employment benefits, but also has some trickier marks on the accrued income scheme. Do your best here and move on! Part (b) focuses on the administration of tax for employees. Administration can represent quick and easy marks in the exam if you have learnt the rules. So make sure you know them. Finally, part (c) looks at intere st and penalties in respect of late payment of a balancing charge. Elements of the self-assessment system are often tested, so make sure you know the implications if deadlines are not met, as well as what the deadlines are. Zune plc provided Poppy with a diesel car (not meeting the real driving emissions 2 (RDE2) standard) and two mobile telephones. These benefits were all payrolled. Poppy had been in partnership with Rose and Teasel, but Teasel resigned as a partner on 6 July 2025; the partners always sharing profits and losses equally. For the year ended 5 April 2026, the partnership had a tax adjusted trading loss (before taking account of capital allowances). The partnership’s only asset was a car used by Poppy which was sold on 31 July 2025. Poppy’s only other income was the accrued in terest from gilts which were purchased on 1 August 2025 and sold on 31 October 2025. The three requirements were all fairly straightforward, so it was surprising that this question was not better answered. Requirement (a) – 10 marks Although the employment aspects of this requirement were well answered by most candidates, a number of candidates struggled to correctly allocate the trading loss. The interaction of capital allowances and loss relief was a particular issue. The calculation of the accrued gilt income also caused problems. • The car benefit should have represented two easy marks, but some candidates omitted the 4% diesel surcharge, and the restriction by 8/12ths (the car only being provided for eight months) was also sometimes incorrectly calculated or omitted altogether. • Most candidates recognised that only on e of the mobile telephones was chargeable, but the 20% basis of tax charge was less well known. --- PAGE 313 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE INCOME TAX AND NATIONAL INSURANCE QUESTIONS: SECTION 6 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 267 With regard to the trading loss, very few candidates appreciated that the balancing allowance from the disposal of the car had to be added to the trading loss before allocating the resultant loss. The balancing allowance was simply: • The brought forward written down value of £8,400 • Less the sale proceeds of £5,400 • Restricted to the business use proportion of 30%. Many candidates overcomplicated this working by claiming allowances prior to the disposal, with others not even realising there was a balancing event. Having calculated a revised trading loss, the profit allocated should have been quite straightforward. However, candidates often wasted time by not restricting their calculation to just Poppy’s share of the £20,400 loss. The shares for Rose and Teasel were not relevant and their calculation did not score any marks. With Poppy receiving one-third of profits and losses for three months, and 50% thereafter, the calculation for 2 marks was simply: (£20,400 × 3/12 × 1/3) + (£20,400 × 9/12 × 1/2) = £9,350 When it comes to calculating accrued interest, candidates should remember that the relevant figures are the nominal value and the interest rate. The gilts had a nominal value of £40,000, an interest rate of 3%, and were owned for three months. The accrued interest calculation for 1.5 marks was therefore: £40,000 at 3% × 3/12 = £300 Requirement (b) – 2 marks This requirement was answered quite poorly. • For the first mark, candidates simply had to say that the related income tax liability is collected under PAYE (or through payroll). • For the second mark, it was necessary to state there is no reporting on form P11D. Although some candidates picked up the first mark, very many candidates then went on to say that reporting on form P11D (or some other form) was required. Requirement (c) – 3 marks This requirement was generally well answered by most candidates. The key point was appreciating that the due date for the bala ncing payment was 31 January 2026, so the payment was made seven months late. The interest charge was therefore £2,600 × 8.5% × 7/12 = £129 for 1.5 marks. A few candidates used the official rate of interest rather than the rate for underpaid tax. As regards penalties, there were two 5% charges; the first for being one month late and the second for being six months late. Candidates should realise that where a requireme nt is just for three marks, then no more than two or three short calculations or sentences are required. Also, answers should be related to the information provided, so a long, detailed, explanation of the interest and penalty rules in general is not going to score well. --- PAGE 314 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 268 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 100 KAZUO Key answer tips It is important to read the scenario and attempt each section of the requirement on its own, making clear which tax you are calculating when a question tests multiple taxes. For part (c), the withdrawal of the income is a few years later when his other income is reduced. This will impact the level of tax that is applicable. He was employed at a gross annual salary of £200,000 (so an additional rate taxpayer) but planned to retire on 5 April 2029. At that point, Kazou’s income will reduce to gross a nnual pension income of £55,000 (so a higher rate taxpayer). Kazuo was going to undertake £40,000 of work on a freelance basis during the year ended 5 April 2026, and will do this via a new limited company, Zaoku Ltd. Kazuo was looking at three alternative ways of extracting the profits of Zaoku Ltd: Alternative 1: After allowing for corporation tax, Kazuo will withdraw the entire net of tax profits as dividends during the tax year 2025/26. Alternative 2: Kazuo will be paid gross directors' remuneration of £8,000 and Zaoku Ltd will make a pension contribution of £32,000 into a company occupational pension scheme on Kazuo's behalf during the tax year 2025/26. Alternative 3: The net of tax profits will be left undrawn in Zaoku Ltd until the tax year 2029/30 when Kazuo has retired. He will then withdraw the entire net of tax amount as dividends in the tax year 2029/30. Although there were a number of perfect answers, many candidates found this question quite challenging. One particular problem was that candidates did not appreciate that part (c) was essentially the same as part (a), but set a few years ahead with a lower tax rate. This future setting confused a significant minority of candidates, with a number calculating income and taxes over several years. However, the question clearly stated that the freelance work would only last for just one year, from 6 April 2025 to 5 April 2026. Requirement (a) – 3 marks This requirement was generally fairly well answered, and there were many perfect answers. Although candidates had the option of using a full calculation approach, working at the margin was easier and quicker. There was also less scope for making arithmetical errors. Unless opting for a full computation approach, the only relevance of Kazuo’s salary of £200,000 was to establish the rate of tax applicable (and it was stated that Kazuo was an additional rate taxpayer in any case). However, a number of candidates included this amount within their corporation tax computation, and this then had a knock-on effect throughout the remainder of the answer. If using a working at the margin approach for the income tax calculation, this was simply (for two marks): £40,000 (freelance earnings) – £7,600 (corporation tax as calculated) – £500 (dividend nil rate band) multiplied by the dividend additional tax rate of 39.35% Common problems included using the gross earnings (rather than the net of tax figure) and using an incorrect rate of tax. Given the rates of tax are provided, it made no sense to lose a half-mark by carelessly using, for example, 39.55% instead of 39.35%. --- PAGE 317 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE INCOME TAX AND NATIONAL INSURANCE QUESTIONS: SECTION 6 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 271 Requirement (b) – 4 marks This requirement caused the most problems, although it was more straightforward than many candidates appreciated. Corporation tax: Paying the director’s remuneration and making the pension contribution simply reduced Zaoku Ltd’s taxable total profits (and corporation tax liability) to £0 (£40,000 – £8,000 – £32,000). Most candidates picked up the deduction for the director’s remuneration, but the deduction for the pension contribution was generally overlooked. Income tax: With a working at the margin approach , the income tax liability was simply £8,000 at 45% = £3,600. The company pension contribution was an exempt benefit, and, since it was paid by Zaoku Ltd, did not extend Kazuo’s tax bands as was often stated by candidates. NICs: With gross directors' remuneration of just £8,000, there were no class 1 NICs given earnings were less than the lower threshold. Many candidates included the completely separate salary of £200,000, and therefore calcul ated class 1 NICs at the rate of 2%. This is why it is so important to read through the question carefully. Comparison: When it came to the comparison with alternative 1, many candidates compared the income tax and NICs, but forgot to include the corporation tax figures. This should have been an easy one mark, as the mark was given provided a candidate made the comparison using whatever figures they had calculated. Another common mistake was to make a comparison based on a full computation approach with one done using a working at the margin approach. It should have been apparent that such a tax difference was not realistic. Many candidates wasted time by redoing their part (a) figures instead of just picking then up from part (a). Requirement (c) – 3 marks There were a number of very good answers for this requirement. However, as already mentioned, many candidates did not appreciate that part (c) was essentially the same as part (a), but set a few years ahead with the dividend higher tax rate being applicable (rather than the additional rate). Full marks could have been obtained with the following working: £31,900 (£40,000 – £7,600 – £500) at 5.6% (39.35% – 33.75%) = £1,786. One fairly common mistake was to either ignore the corporation tax (which was unchanged) or to calculate a new (and different) corporation tax figure. The important thing when confronted by a different style of question to what has been practiced (and this will often be the case with the higher skills questions) is to not panic, read the question carefully to see what is required, and to appreciate that if workings become too long or complicated, the requirement has not been properly understood. --- PAGE 318 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 272 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 101 SHELDON Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor Key answer tips This question requires a full income tax computation, covering employment income with various benefits and property income. This question was very well answered, with a number of perfect responses. However, quite a few candidates failed to achieve fairly easy marks due to poor examination technique and/or not reading the question carefully enough. Although there were various ways of approaching this question, the easiest one was to have a main computation with workings for employment income and for property income. Of course, many candidates had a lot more workings than this, which would have taken more time and made it more difficult to keep track of all the relevant figures. As regards poor examination technique, one of the main problems here was not showing workings. If workings are shown, marks will still be given even if an arithmetical mistake is made. For example, one candidate incorrectly showed the beneficial loan as ((£80,000 – £72,000)/2) × 3.75% × 8/12 = £100. The correct calculation was ((£80,000 + £72,000)/2) × 3.75% × 8/12 = £1,900. However, because they had shown their workings, they were awarded 1 of the available 1.5 marks. As regards not reading the question carefu lly enough, there were two quite common mistakes made that were costly in terms of marks: • Luqe Ltd provided Sheldon with living accommodation. Even though the question stated that living accommodation was provided throughout the tax year, a number of candidates misread the subsequent statement that Sheldon first moved into the property on 1 January 2025. They took this to be the 1 January during the tax year in question (which would have been 1 January 2026) and then restricted living accommodation benefits by 3/12ths. • For the property income expenses, it was stated that Sheldon’s expenditure was £35,800 for the tax year. This figure included three amounts, only one of which was disallowable (£1,600 for legal fees in relation to the grant of a five-year lease). The deduction was therefore a quite straightforward £35,800 – £1,600 = £34,200. However, many candidates either ignored the total figure of £35,800, deducted £35,800 along with some or all the other fi gures, or deducted an adjusted version of £35,800 along with some or all the other figures. There were two marks for the correct deduction, but the incorrect variations scored poorly. Candidates should avoid putting detailed workings within the one cell because it is too easy to make a mistake with the syntax. Referring to the beneficial loan working again, one mistake that cropped up several times was (£80,000 + £72,000/2) = £116,000 rather than the correct ((£80,000 + £72,000)/2) = £76,000. Although candidates are not usually penalised for such obvious errors, it will be an issue where more complicated workings are involved. Candidates who rush their response, can sometime s fail to spot the obvious. Before taking account of benefits or other income, Sheldon had a gross annual salary of £126,000. This level of income by itself meant that Sheldon was not entitled to any personal allowance and was an additional rate taxpayer. The personal allowance was sometimes given regardless, and the tax rate applied to Sheldon’s dividend income was sometimes not 39.35%. Looking at some of the other half marks on this question: • The half mark for the use of Luqe Ltd’s company gym being an exempt benefit was picked up by virtually every candidate. --- PAGE 322 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 276 KAPLAN PUBLISHING • The half mark for the living accommodation running costs of £850 was sometimes not given because this figure was deducted rather than treated as a benefit. • The half mark for deducting the £3,000 (£250 × 12) that Sheldon paid towards the living accommodation was sometimes not given because 12 months of payment were not used. • The half mark for the medical insurance benefit of £890 was sometimes not given due to this incorrectly being treated as an exempt benefit. • The half mark for the reimbursed business expenditure of £600 was sometimes not given because this was either treated as taxable or deductible. Not achieving a few half marks may not sound that serious, but if done a few times it can easily be the difference between a marginal fail and a pass mark. 102 KAGAN Key answer tips This question is a typical ‘higher skills’ quest ion where the focus wa s spread across three taxes, IHT, CGT and income tax. Although fairly well answered, many candidates used valuable time doing full before and after tax computations. Kagan was clearly an additional rate taxpayer, so all that was required was to calculate the additional rate tax due on the dividend income and then add it to the provided figure of tax on the employment income. Part (b)(i) for 1 mark required an explanation as to why little or no capital gains tax would have been payable if Kagan had sold some of his inherited shares. This was because assets are inherited at the value at the time of the deceased’s death. If these assets are sold soon after being inherited, there will generally be a minimal increase in value (this fact was stated in the question), so any gain is likely to be covered by the annual exempt amount. It was pleasing to see that this part was well answered by those candidates who appreciated the tax treatment. Part (b)(ii) for 6 marks required a calculation of Kagan’s revised income tax liability for the tax year 2025/26 if he sold so me of his inherited shares and made the four alternative investments. This section was re asonably well answered, but several points should be noted: The question stated that a full tax computation was required, so exempt items (pension lump sum, premium bond prizes and the interest from the ISA) should simply have been listed within the main computation and indicated as such by the use of zero (0) – not by an explanation. • The non-availability of the personal allowa nce should have been indicated in the same manner. There was no need to justify the non-availability given the level of Kagan’s income. • Although there might only be a ½ mark av ailable for recognising an exemption, it is important to know the various exemptions so that time is not spent producing unnecessary, and more complicated workings – such as applying the savings income nil rate band where the interest from the ISA was included as savings income. Part (c) for 2 marks required candidates to state for each of the four alternative investments whether the investment would reduce Kagan’s potential inheritance tax liability compared to him retaining the inherited shares. Unfort unately, this section was not well answered. Candidates need to remember, that unlike other taxes, there are few exemptions from inheritance tax. Therefore, the replacement of the quoted shares with either premium bonds, an ISA or freehold property would not have changed the value of Kagan’s chargeable estate. However, the investment in the pension fund (which is not withdrawn) would have been outside of Kagan’s estate, thereby reducing his potential IHT liability. --- PAGE 325 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE INCOME TAX AND NATIONAL INSURANCE QUESTIONS: SECTION 6 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 279 103 ESME Key answer tips Part (a) of this question is a standard income tax computation, involving employment income with various benefits as well as dividend income. Those candidates who made sure that they understood the scenario and worked carefully through each calculation had no difficulty answering this section. As warned in previous reports, where a tax figure is given for one of the scenarios (in this case, the corporation tax figure), candidates sh ould never attempt to recalculate the figure for themselves. All this does is use up valuable time. As regards the conclusion, this should have just been a calculation of the tax difference between the two scenarios. Those candidates who calculated the tax liability for a personal purchase and then attempted to adjust the figures for a corporate purchase invariably ended up with a very confused answer. The personal purchase required candidates to apply the restriction whereby relief for 100% of property income finance costs is restricted to the basic rate. Working through past examination questions will help candidates familiarise themselves with the best approach to be taken when answering questions which examine more than one tax. Bertie had previously withdrawn a high level of director’s remuneration from Rebite Ltd, but is considering more beneficial alternative arrangements for the tax year 2025/26. Existing arrangements: Bertie will be paid gross director’s remuneration of £75,000 and will then use his private car for business mileage (b eing paid a mileage allowance for doing so). He will make personal pension contributions of £25,000 (gross). Beneficial arrangements: Instead of director’s remuneration, Bertie will be paid dividends of £35,000. He will also be provided with an electric company car which will be leased by Rebite Ltd. Instead of Bertie personally making personal pension contributions, Rebite Ltd will make pension contributions of £25,000 into a company pension scheme on his behalf. Provided candidates kept the two sets of information separate, this question as a whole was generally very well answered. One particular problem however, was that some candidates treated Rebite Ltd’s trading profit of £340,000 as personal income. Although the general approach when marking is that candidates only lose marks once under the “own figure rule”, having such a high level of income completely distorted the income tax calculations, with the result that several half-marks were sometimes not able to be awarded. With this style of question, it is very import ant to use appropriate headings so that it is obvious which aspect of the requirement is being answered. --- PAGE 338 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 292 KAPLAN PUBLISHING Although a higher skills question, candidates were instructed to produce full income tax and NIC computations. Candidates seem to prefer this approach (compared to working at the margin), and this largely explains the very good performance. There were many perfect answers to both aspects of requirement (a). Existing arrangements In regard to the existing arrangements, a number of candidates did not appreciate that the allowance received by Bertie for business mile age in his private car was tax-free with no expense claim possible. This was because the a llowance of 45 pence per mile is exactly the amount of authorised mileage allowance permitted by HM Revenue & Customs. When it came to the income tax computation, a fairly common mistake was to not appreciate that Bertie’s liability was solely at 20% given the extent that the basic rate band was extended by his personal pension contributions. With the calculation of employee class 1 NIC, quite a few candidates did not use Bertie’s gross director’s remuneration of £75,000 as the limiting figure. Instead, the taxable income figure was often used, or a figure adjusted for personal pension contributions and/or the mileage allowance. Beneficial arrangements In regard to the beneficial arrangements, there were various mistakes: • Normal tax rates were sometimes applied instead of the dividend tax rates; • It was not appreciated that with just dividend income, there would be no NIC payable; • The car benefit – although correctly calculated – was sometimes shown as separate to the main income tax calculation (the basic rate of 20% was then applied, even though the benefit was clearly covered by Bertie’s personal allowance); and • Rebite Ltd’s pension contributions on Bertie’s behalf were taken into account despite being an exempt benefit. Again, there were many perfect answers to requirement (b). One particular problem was that a number of candidates recalculated Rebite Ltd’s corporation tax liability under the existing arrangements, despite being instructed not to do so – this figure was being provided. If the correct figure was recalculated, this was just a case of some time being wasted. However, an incorrect calculation meant both wasted time and the inability to get the half-mark. This is why it is so important to read through the question carefully, especially the requirements along with any guidance notes. The computation itself was fairly straightforward, and half the marks would have been given if just the trading profit of £340,000 was taxed at 25%, with this figure then compared to the given corporation tax liability under the existing arrangements. To get full marks, it was also necessary to deduct the leasing costs and the pension contributions. The dividends paid to Bertie were irrelevant, although some candidates insisted on deducting them. This is why question practice is so important because this is the type of mistake which when made once, candidates learn not to repeat. --- PAGE 339 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE INCOME TAX AND NATIONAL INSURANCE QUESTIONS: SECTION 6 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 293 INCOME TAX BASICS AND INCOME FROM SELF-EMPLOYMENT 107 TRIPLE A LTD Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor Key answer tips This question requires a comprehe nsive calculation of tax liabilities for both the individuals and the company, and then a comparison to determine the most tax-efficient structure. It is im portant to appreciate the interactions that can arise in a higher skills question, and reading published articles and practising exam standard questions will help to this end. Requirement (i) This was a very straightforward computation provided candidates ignored the pension contributions made by Triple A Ltd, and used the correct rate of tax for the dividend income. Many candidates did not do this, thereby missing the very easy mark. --- PAGE 342 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 296 KAPLAN PUBLISHING Because all three directors had the same income, the correct approach was to do the one income tax calculation and to then multiply the end result by three. Quite a number of candidates wasted time (even if it was just a matter of copy and paste) by producing three separate, but exactly the same, computations. Requirement (ii) The corporation tax working for Triple A Ltd was somewhat more difficult, although there were a number of perfect answers. Candidates had to start with the company’s taxable total profits (figure provided), then deduct the total director’s remuneration, class 1 employer NICs and pension scheme contributions (all these figures were provided). It was necessary, however, to multiply the provided figures for director’s remuneration and pension scheme contributions by three – the number of directors. Dividends should be ignored, although quite a few candidates deducted them. Another mistake sometimes made was to deduct the class 1 employee NICs as well as, or instead of, the employer NICs. If this was done, the half mark for correctly deducting just the employer NICs was not given. Provided the correct figures were deducted, candidates would then have had a revised taxable total profits figure of below £50,000. The corporation tax calculation was therefore at the single rate of 19%. If any of the figures were missed, candidates would have been faced with a more difficult marginal relief calculation for equivalent marks. With no dividend income, this could have of course been calculated as £50,000 at 19%, with the balance of profits charged at 26.5%. Requirement (iii) The comparison meant pulling to gether figures from both the scenario as well as ones calculated. The comparison was between the total tax and NIC liabilities for the partners if they had continued to trade as a partnership (these figures were all provided) and the total income tax liabilities of the directors (calculated), the corporation tax liability of Triple A Ltd (calculated) and the class 1 employee and employer NICs (figures provided). Most candidates achieved at least some marks here, with many gaining the full 1.5 marks. Q4 • Official Past Question (Income Tax & NIC)
+10 XP Income Tax & NIC

March 2019 OT question
Hana was UK resident in the tax year 2024/25. He worked full time in Egypt in the tax year
2025/26.
What is the maximum number of days which Hana can spend in the UK and be treated as
automatically not resident in the UK for the tax year 2025/26?

4 C Examiner’s report This question examines the third automatic non-UK residency test. For an individual to meet this test, and therefore be treated as automatically not resident in the UK for the tax year 2025/26, they would have to work full-time overseas and spend less than 91 days in the UK. Therefore, because Hana worked full-time in Egypt throughout 2025/26, he will be treated as automatically not resident in the UK for the tax year as long as he spends no more than 90 days in the UK. The correct answer is therefore C, however, answer option A was most commonly chosen. This would be the correct answer using the sufficient ties tests. However, the sufficient ties tests are only used to determine residence status if none of the automatic non-UK residence tests (and none of the automatic UK residence tests) is met. This suggests that candidates may not have be en familiar enough with the residence tests and the procedure to determine residence.
OFFICIAL KEY: C
This answer has been extracted and verified against Kaplan official sittings for Finance Act 2025 sittings.

Tutorial note Income generated from assets which are owned jointly is split 50:50 between spouses regardless of the actual ownership percentage, unless an election is made to use the actual ownership percentage. It would not be beneficial to Zara to make a joint election to HMRC specifying their actual ownership share in the property. In doing so, Zara would be taxed on 75% of the property income, i.e. £15,000 (20,000 × 75%). This would increase Zara’s tax liability for the tax year 2025/26 and it would also mean that more of the income would be taxed at the higher rate of 40%, than under the current 50:50 split.

53 B Examiner’s report This question examines knowledge of the deadlin e for an individual taxpayer to claim relief for a trading loss which they wish to offset in the tax year prior to the tax year in which the loss arose. The correct answer is option B (31 January 2028), as a claim must be made within one year of 31 January following the end of the tax year in which the loss arose. Therefore, as the loss arose in the tax year 2025/26, a claim for relief must be made by 31 January 2028. Option B was the most common answer selected but a significant number of candidates also chose each of the other answer options, suggesting that many candidates were not well prepared for a question on this topic. The second most common answer was option A (31 January 2027) which is the deadline for submitting a personal tax return online for the tax year 2025/26. Candidates may have selected this date as they are familiar with this deadline in relation to the tax year 2025/26 and assumed the deadline for claiming the loss would be the same. Administration deadlines, both for individuals and companies, are an important part of the syllabus and future candidates are reminded of the importance of learning, and being able to distinguish between, the different deadlines as part of their studies. All of them had shares in a company which is taken over. Takeovers can be complicated where there is mixed consideration and many students may have been put off by the opening paragraph. Ho wever, in this question, there is no mixed consideration and it is quite straightforward. They are disposing of their existing shares and have a choice of either cash or shares, but not a mixture of the two. Of the three individuals, one chooses cash and therefore they just have a straightforward disposal of shares for cash. The other two choose shares, which is just a sh are for share exchange with no capital gains tax consequences at that time. The new shares just ‘stand in the shoes’ of the old shares and are deemed to have been acquired at the same cost and at the same time as the original shares. They then dispose of some of the new shares. For the first part, detailed knowledge of the BADR conditions is required. 1 Meets the conditions for BADR Does not meet the conditions for BADR Aloi  Bon  Cherry  Aloi Aloi acquired her shareholding and became a director on 1 January 2015, so the qualifying conditions were met for the 24 months prior to the date of the takeover. (b) Chargeable gains – year ended 31 March 2026 Tutor’s top tips In the absence of guidance on the split of marks you should assume equal weighting is given between the two disposals, and allocate your time accordingly. Q181 • Official Past Question (Inheritance Tax)
+10 XP Inheritance Tax

September 2017 OT question
Cora made a cash gift of £300,000 to her niece on 30 April 2020.
She then made a cash gift of £500,000 to her nephew on 31 May 2021.
Both of these amounts are stated after deducting available exemptions.
Cora subsequently died on 31 October 2025.
What amount of inheritance tax was payable as a result of Cora’s death in respect of the
cash gift of £500,000 to her nephew?

181 C £ £ Gross chargeable amount 500,000 NRB (2025/26) 325,000 Less: GCTs < 7 years before gift (31.5.2014 – 31.5.2021) (300,000) ––––––– (25,000) ––––––– Taxable amount 475,000 ––––––– IHT payable @ 40% 190,000 Less: Taper relief (31.5.2021 – 31.10.2025) (4 – 5 years before death) (40%) (76,000) ––––––– IHT payable on death 114,000 ––––––– 182 £325,000 Both of Gabe’s lifetime gifts are PETs, which are not taxable and will not use any NRB during his lifetime and will become exempt if he lives for seven years following the date of the gift. Seven years prior to his death was 22 November 2018, and since the cash gift to his daughter is before this date it will never become chargeable to IHT and is now exempt. The gift of the painting to his son (£370,000) is within this seven-year period and becomes chargeable using the nil rate band at death (£325,000). In the seven years prior to that gift (12 July 2014 to 12 July 2021) the only gift was the PET to his daughter, which is now exempt, so it does not use any NRB at death. Therefore, the NRB available to the second PET on Gabe’s death is the full £325,000. Tutorial note Note that if the first gift had been a chargeable lifetime transfer (CLT), it would have used some NRB on Gabe’s death.
OFFICIAL KEY: C

for inheritance tax purposes after taking account of all available exemptions?

The annual exemption is offset against the earliest gift in the tax year automatically. The 2025/26 annual exemption is therefore reduced by the amount given to Sameer’s friend, as this was before the gift to the trust. The current year’s annual exemption must be offset prior to the offset of any brought forward amounts. Q185 • Official Past Question (Inheritance Tax)
+10 XP Inheritance Tax

September 2015 OT question
Heng is a wealthy 45 year old who would like to reduce the potential inheritance tax liability
on her estate when she dies.
Which of the following actions will NOT achieve Heng’s aim of reducing the potential
inheritance tax liability on her estate when she dies?

185 A Tutorial note Option A describes the common inheritance tax planning technique of ‘skipping a generation’. This technique can maximise the inheritance available to future generations as a charge to inheritance tax will only arise once, on th e passing of the estate residue to Heng’s grandchildren. If the residue had been left to Heng’s children and they subsequently gifted the assets to their children, two charges to inheritance tax would arise. That being said, skipping a generation woul d not reduce Heng’s potential inheritance tax liability on death as legacies left to both children and grandchildren are equally chargeable.
OFFICIAL KEY: A
