The requirement for part (a) was to calculate the IHT payable as a result of a taxpayer’s death, and to state who was responsible for paying the tax. The taxpayer had made (1) a chargeable lifetime transfer (more than seven years before death), (2) a potentially exempt transfer and (3) another chargeable lifetime transfer. A quick review of the information given should have indicated that no lifetime tax would have been paid (this fact was actually stated in respect of the second chargeable lifetime transfer) and that taper relief was not relevant (given that none of the gifts were between four and seven years of death). However, many candidates dedicated a lot of time to establishing this. Candidates should read through the question carefully before they begin their calculations. Part (b) required an explanation as to why it might have been beneficial if the taxpayer had left a portion of their estate to his nephew rather than to his brother. This aspect was well answered, with most candidates appreciating the basic IHT planning of avoiding a double charge to tax. The IHT planning in part (c) was less well understood. It was necessary to explain why it might be advantageous to make lifetime gifts even when such gifts are made within seven years of death. The main advantage here is that the value of the gift is fixed at the time it is made, so no IHT is payable on the increase in value between making the gift and the time of death. Taper relief may also be available. --- PAGE 519 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE INHERITANCE TAX QUESTIONS: SECTION 8 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 473 212 JESSICA Key answer tips This question requires the calculation of CGT and IHT on gifts made to a trust, as well as the income tax implications of these gifts. It can be daunting when multiple taxes are covered in one question, however the requirements are completely distinct and the income tax information is separate in the question. The challenge is therefore to distinguish the information needed for CGT and IHT and to correctly apply the rules for valuing unquoted shares for IHT purposes and the CGT rules for gifts. For the capital gains tax calculation, pay close attention to how the market value of unquoted shares is determined. When calculating the lifetime inheritance tax, remember the 'loss to the donor' (diminution in value) principle. Also ensure you use the correct IHT rates for lifetime transfers. Finally, for the income tax reduction, focus on the change in Jessica's taxable income categories due to the gifts. In order to calculate the answers in the time allowed for just three marks, it will be necessary to work in the margin, rather than producing full income tax computations. Make sure to apply the correct tax rates for savings and dividends for an additional rate taxpayer. On 6 April 2025, she had made a lifetime gift consisting of both shares and cash to a trust, with the funds then being held for the benefit of her two grandchildren aged three and four. Although this question was well answered, the fact that the same share information had to be used for both capital gains tax and inheritance tax purposes often caused confusion. This is despite a similar example being included in the higher skills, chargeable gains and inheritance tax articles. It is important to appreciate the interactions that can arise in a higher skills question, and reading publis hed articles and practising exam standard questions will help to this end. Requirement (a) The relevant information to pull out from the question is that Jessica made a gift of 100,000 £1 ordinary shares in Valuable Ltd to the trust. With Valuable Ltd having a share capital of 250,000 £1 ordinary shares, the gift represents a 40% shareholding, so the relevant deemed proceeds figure is based on £4 per share. The shares were acquired at a £1 par value. Therefore, the gain is simply 100,000 × £3 (£4 – £1) = £300,000 (for 2 marks). Deduct the annual exempt amount, multiply by the higher capital gains tax rate (since Jessica is an additional rate taxpayer), and that gives the capital gains tax figure. Provided the valuation basis is understood, that should be a very easy and quick 3 marks. The big problem for many candidates, of course, was that they used an inheritance tax basis of valuation. A common error was to calculate the inheritance tax value (£900,000 – part (b)) and then deduct the correct cost figure of £100,000 (100,000 at £1). This would have wasted a minute or two on the erroneous calculation. Requirement (b) The diminution in value of Jessica’s estate wa s a cash element of £250,000 (for one mark), and the 100,000 £1 ordinary shares in Valuab le Ltd. Before the transfer, Jessica owned 150,000 shares; a 60% shareholding valued at £7 per share. After the transfer, Jessica owned 50,000 shares; a 20% shareholding valued at £3 per share. The diminution in value from the gift of shares was therefore (150,000 at £7) – (50,000 at £3) = £900,000 (for 2 marks). --- PAGE 522 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 476 KAPLAN PUBLISHING The total value of the transfer was therefore £1,150,000 (£250,000 + £900,000). It was then just a case of deducting the full nil rate band of £325,000, with lifetime tax calculated at the rate of 20% (since the trust paid the inheritance tax arising). This requirement was quite well answered, although a very common mistake was to exclude the £50,000 held within cash ISAs from the cash element of £250,000. Even though the requirement was to ignore the inheritance tax annual exemption, quite a few candidates still deducted this. Despite the scenario clearly stating that the trust paid the inheritance tax arising, a number of candidates grossed up the tax due using a rate of 20/80ths. Requirement (c) The gift impacted on Jessica’s savings income and her dividend income. Savings income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have received savings income of £6,250 on the cash held during the tax year, of which £1,250 would have been from ISAs. Dividend income: If the gift had not been made, Jessica would have had dividend income of £24,000. This was reduced to £8,000 as a result of making the gift of shares. There were many perfect answers to this requirement, although answers were often more complicated than they needed to be. Savings income: The ISA intere st was not relevant (being exempt), so the income tax reduction was simply £5,000 (£6,250 – £1,250) at 45% = £2,250 for 1.5 marks. Any attempt to include the personal allowance made it impossible to score full marks. Dividend income: Here, the income tax reduction was £16,000 (£24,000 – £8,000) at 39.35% = £6,296 for 1.5 marks. The dividend nil rate band often caused unnecessary complications, although full marks were still available if the nil rate band was deducted from both ‘before gift’ and ‘after gift’ computations. Candidates should be careful to use the correct tax rates which are clearly shown in the tax tables available in the exam. --- PAGE 523 --- KAPLAN PUBLISHING 477 Section 9 ANSWERS TO PRACTICE CORPORATION TAX QUESTIONS PRACTICE SECTION A OBJECTIVE TEST QUESTIONS CORPORATION TAX BASICS AND ADMINISTRATION 213 Accounting period 1 March 2025 to 31 March 2025  1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 Corporation tax due FY2024  FY2025 Examiner’s report An accounting period starts when the company becomes liable to corporation tax, in this case the company started to earn interest (on which it will pay corporation tax) on the 1 March 2025. An accounting period will finish when the company starts to trade and this will start a new accounting period. Therefore, the first accounting period will be from 1 March 2025 to 31 March 2025. A financial year (FY) starts on 1 April and ends on 31 March and is identified by the calendar year in which it begins. In this case the accounting period 1 March to 31 March 2025 falls within the FY2024 (starting on 1 April 2024 and ending on 31 March 2025). The accounting period from 1 April 2025 to 31 March 2026 is the second accounting period for corporation tax purposes (when trade starts and running to the maximum period of 12 months) and that falls into FY2025 (starting on 1 April 2025).
OFFICIAL KEY: B

2024 on 15 March 2026.
What is the deadline for HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC) to start a compliance check
enquiry into Somily Ltd’s corporation tax return for the year ended 31 December 2024?

214 A Tutorial note If a company files its return on time HMRC has 12 months from the date of actual delivery of the return to give notice of a compliance check. If the return is submitted late, notice must be given within 12 months from the 31 January, 30 April, 31 July or 31 October next following the actual date of delivery of the tax return to HMRC (i.e. within 12 months of the next ‘quarter day’). --- PAGE 524 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 478 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 215 Resident Not resident A Ltd, a company incorporated in the UK, with its central management and control exercised in the UK  B Ltd, a company incorporated overseas, with its central management and control exercised in the UK  C Ltd, a company incorporated in the UK, with its central management and control exercised overseas  D Ltd, a company incorporated overseas, with its central management and control exercised overseas 

Which of the three companies will be treated as resident in the UK for corporation tax
purposes?

216 C Tutorial note Companies are UK resident if they are incorporated in the UK or if they are centrally managed and controlled in the UK. Xebec Inc is managed and controlled in the UK. Q227 • Official Past Question (Corporation Tax)
+10 XP Corporation Tax

December 2020 OT question
Giant Ltd is a large company, and therefore pays its corporation tax by instalments.
For the eight-month period ended 31 August 2025, the company estimated that its
corporation tax liability would be £400,000.
What would Giant Ltd’s first corporation tax instalment be in respect of the eight-month
period ended 31 August 2025, and what is the due date of this instalment.

227 D Tutorial note A large company is required to pay its final instalment of corporation tax by the 14th day of the 4th month after the end of the accounting period (AP). Note that for a 12-month AP this is 16 months after the start of the AP. Where an AP is less than 12 months, the first instalment is due by the 14th day of the 7th month after the start of the AP. Subsequent instalments are due at 3 monthly intervals thereafter, until the date of the final instalment is reached. For an eight-month AP instalments are due on the 14th day of months 7, 10 and 12 (the last being 4 months after the end of the AP). For this scenario, that is 14 July 2025, 14 October 2025 and 14 December 2025. The first two instalments are calculated as 3/8 × corporation tax liability (£400,000 × 3/8 = £150,000). The final instalment will be 2/8 × corporation tax liability. Examiner’s report A number of candidates selected B £100,000 on 14 July 2025, which is the correct due date however the instalment amount (calculated as £400,000 × 3/12, giving £100,000) is incorrect because £100,000 would be the amount payable if the period had been 12 months (rather than eight months) long. RELIEF FOR TRADING LOSSES
OFFICIAL KEY: D
This answer has been extracted and verified against Kaplan official sittings for Finance Act 2025 sittings.

Q239 • Official Past Question (Corporation Tax)
+10 XP Corporation Tax

September/December 2024 OT question
Xtra Ltd bought 60% of the ordinary share capital of Yak Ltd on 31 October 2024 and 80% of
the ordinary share capital of Zeus Ltd on 31 March 2025.
For the year ended 31 December 2025, Xtra Ltd made a trading profit of £240,000 and Yak Ltd
made a trading profit of £120,000. Zeus Ltd made a trading loss of £180,000 for the year
ended 31 December 2025.
Which TWO of the following statements are correct in respect of the potential group relief
claims which can be made for the year ended 31 December 2025?

239 A and D Tutorial note Group relief can only be claimed for the period when Zeus Ltd was in the Xtra Ltd group, i.e. from 1 April 2025. Group relief is therefore available for nine months in the year ended 31 December 2025. It is restricted to the lower of the available profits in Xtra Ltd and the available losses in Zeus Ltd for that nine-month period. Zeus Ltd can therefore surrender the lower of £180,000 (£240,000 × 9/12) and £135,000 (£180,000 × 9/12) to Xtra Ltd. Yak Ltd is not in a 75% group with Xtra Ltd and Zeus Ltd, and so cannot claim group relief for the corresponding accounting period.
OFFICIAL KEY: A

Q243 • Official Past Question (Corporation Tax)
+10 XP Corporation Tax

Telephone Ltd prepares accounts to 31 March each year. Throughout the year ended
31 March 2026 Telephone Ltd owned 62% of Desk Ltd, 75% of Chair Ltd, 55% of Floor Ltd
(a dormant company) and 100% of Window Inc (resident overseas). Telephone Ltd acquired

limits for calculating the corporation tax of Telephone Ltd for the year ended 31 March
2026?

243 C Tutorial note There are five associated companies (Telephone Ltd, Desk Ltd, Chair Ltd, Window Inc and Blind Ltd) for the purposes of adjusting the upper and lower limits (for tax rate purposes) for the year ended 31 March 2026. Associated companies are those companies that are under the control of Telephone Ltd (i.e. Telephone Ltd owns, either directly or indirectly, more than 50% of the company’s ordinary share capital). The upper and lower limits (for tax rate purposes) are adjusted for the number of associated companies in the accounting period, regardless of when in that period they were acquired or disposed. Therefore, Blind Ltd is included for the year ended 31 March 2026. Overseas companies are included but dormant companies are excluded.

In contrast, tax avoidance involves the minimisation of tax liabilities by the use of any lawful means. If Harbour Ltd extends its accounting period in order to save corporation tax, then HMRC will not view this as tax evasion because it is quite lawful for the company to prepare accounts up to whatever accounting date it wishes. The corporation tax figure follows after the main computation. There are two very important points here: Negative figures should be clearly shown by entering them as such on the spreadsheet. It is very difficult for markers to pick up negative figures if all figures are shown positive, with the total calculated within the cell on the lines of A1 + A2 – A3 + A4. It is also very easy to make mistakes using this approach. If negative figures are entered, the total is simply SUM(A1:A4). Requirement (a) – 10 marks As the note states, answers should commence with the operating profit. Any different approach makes an answer quite difficult to mark, especially an answer which attempts to rewrite the statement of profit or loss. Figures should not be combined. For example, the amortisation add back of £1,300 and the lease premium deduction of £806 should not be shown as £494, especially as £494 was also a fairly common incorrect answer for the lease premium deduction. It should also be noted that since the lease premium consists of a payment, it simply cannot result in an income entry. There are a couple of aspects which require obvious care: • Interest paid in the statement of profit or loss is £24,600. Accruals at the beginning and end of the period are £20,500 and £12, 300 respectively. The correct figure (on a payable basis) to deduct in working out the trading profit is therefore £24,600 – £20,500 + £12,300 = £16,400. • With the property business income, the rent has been received for six months, but the insurance paid for 12 months. Given the four-month accounting period, the calculation is therefore (£15,600 × 4/6) – (£1,800 × 4/12) = £9,800. Question practice will eliminate mistakes such as giving an annual exempt amount (which is not available for companies) against the chargeable gain, thereby losing a very easy ½ mark. Also, candidates should appreciate that both the annual investment allowance and [first year] allowance are given for the same asset if the annual investment allowance expenditure limit is exceeded. In this case, the annual investment expenditure limit was reduced to £1,000,000 × 4/12 = £333,333 because of the four-month accounting period. Requirement (b)(i) – 3 marks The fact that this requirement is just for 3 marks, together with the use of ‘briefly’ should be a very good indication that only a short set of answers is required. This is why it is important to make use of the model answers since candidates’ answers should not be any longer. If tax evasion and tax avoidance are muddled up, the available marks are obviously going to be lost, so candidates should think first, writ e second. The key point is that tax evasion is illegal, whereas tax avoidance is legal. As regards Harbour Ltd extending its accounting period, the company can do this provided company law requirements are met (and these are not relevant to the tax examination). Therefore, candidates cannot expect to get the full mark available if there [are] any caveats to their answer. The question involved three unrelated companies; Deimos Ltd, Elara Ltd and Fenrir Ltd. Requirement (a) – 2 marks There was one mark for the period 1 May 2024 to 30 April 2025, a half mark for the period 1 May 2025 to 30 September 2025 (the period of account to 30 September 2025 being split into two accounting periods), and a half mark for the period from 1 October 2025 (from the date of the final financial statements) to 28 February 2026 (completion of winding up). This requirement was generally well answered, although many candidates either did not appreciate that there was an accounting period running from 1 October 2025 to 28 February 2026, or they had just the one period running from 1 May 2025 to 28 February 2026. Requirement (b) – 9 marks With this type of answer containing additions and deductions, candidates should be careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions included as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. It is then just a matter of using the SUM function to get to a figure for taxable total profits. Candidates who added up their total figure on a cell-by-cell basis (e.g. A1 + A2 + A3 etc) invariably had problems when it came to negative entries, and it was sometimes difficult for markers to determine whether a figure was a plus or a minus. None of the adjustments or entries really needed separate workings. The capital allowances were simply £220,000 at 100%, and £30,000 at 18% (for one mark in each case), and the gain was calculated as the proceeds of £204,000 less the reinvestment of £168,000 (1.5 marks). This requirement was generally very well answ ered. The only aspects which consistently caused problems were the two interest figures and the chargeable gain. It was somewhat surprising to see a number of candidates adding the figure for interest payable and deducting the figure for interest receivable. Such carelessness cost a half mark in each case. With the chargeable gain, it was clearly stated that Elara Ltd had made a claim to rollover the gain, so this should have represented a fairly easy 1.5 marks. Many candidates forgot to make the deduction for the qualifying charitable donations, even where they had correctly added them back earlier in their computation. Requirement (c) – 4 marks There were quite a number of perfect answers to this requirement, although a number of candidates did not appreciate that payment of a dividend and the advance rental payment would not impact Fenrir Ltd’s corporation tax liability for year ending 31 March 2026. This is because dividends are paid out of post-tax profits, and (given the accruals basis of accounts preparation) rent paid in advance would not be deductible for the year ended 31 March 2026. Having worked out the adjustments, candidates then needed to calculate the tax saving. This could either be done by multiplying the adjustment by the corporation tax rate of 25%, or working out a revised corporation tax liability and comparing this to the previous liability. Well prepared candidates were able to answer this requirement quickly (a benefit of question practice), scoring a fairly straightforward four marks and saving time. However, a correct answer for the car – along with the 25% tax saving – was sufficient to score half of the marks. --- PAGE 564 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 518 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 258 VENUS LTD Key answer tips This is a fairly standard corporation tax question, with just one requirement for 15 marks. Requirement (a) – 15 marks Commencing with the operating profit, candidates were required to adjust for the following: Disallowable expenditure (2.5 marks): There were five items to consider, and these were all non-allowable. The majority of candidates correctly adjusted for four or five of the items, although the amortisation and/or the qualif ying charitable donations were sometimes missed. For this style of question, it is very important that candidates clearly indicate whether items are being added or deducted. A single column layout is therefore recommended. Leasehold premium (3 marks): Many candidates had no difficulty calculating the correct deduction for the grant of a 12-year lease. One common mistake, however, was to work out the non-chargeable portion of the lease (£96,000 × 2% × (12 – 1) = £21,120) and then use that for the basis of the lease deduction rather than working out the chargeable portion (£96,000 – £21,120 = £74,880). Although most candidates appreciated that the chargeable portion then had to be divided by the number of years of the lease (12 years), quite a few did not then apply the 6/12ths restriction; the lease being granted on 1 October 2025. An alternative approach to calculating the chargeable portion of the lease was £96,000 × (51 – 12)/50 = £74,880. If using this approach, candidates needed to take care as the incorrect number of years (51 years and 12 years) were often used. It was also important to realise that the final result had to be deducted in the main computation. Regardless of approach, it is not recommended to attempt the entire working within the one spreadsheet cell. For example, missing the brackets on £96,000 × 51 – 12/50 would give an answer of £4,896,000. Provided the correct wo rkings are shown, appropriate marks will be awarded even if a candidate makes an arithmetical error. Without workings, it can be difficult determining what the candidate’s intention is. Capital allowances (5.5 marks): There were quite a lot of marks for a capital allowances computation, so care was needed. It was pleasing to see many perfect answers, but some candidates struggled here. It was necessary to decide whether an asset purchase qualified for the 100% annual investment allowance, and, if not qualifying , whether the purchase went into the main pool or the special rate pool. The aspect which caused most difficulty was the disposal of the car purchased during the same year. The correct treatment was to add the addition and to deduct the disposal proceeds from the special rate pool. However, many candidates kept this car separate and calculated a balancing adjustment. Other income (2 marks): The other income consisted of bank interest (it was necessary to add in a year end accrual), dividends from an 80% UK subsidiary company (this was exempt income) and a chargeable gain (the profit before taking account of the indexation allowance was also given). Once again, there were a lot of perfect answers here. Typical mistakes included deducting the bank interest accrual, treating the dividend as taxable, and using the pre-indexed gain or deducting the annual exempt amount of £3,000. This is why question practice is so important because these are the type of mistakes which if made once, are less likely to be repeated. --- PAGE 568 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 522 KAPLAN PUBLISHING Deductions (1.5 marks): After adding it back to trading profits earlier, the qualifying charitable donation now had to be deducted from total profits for a half mark. A group relief deduction was also available in respect of a trading loss made by the 80% UK subsidiary company. There was one mark for this, but only a half mark if not deducted at the correct point in the main computation or if the loss was restricted to 80%. Corporation tax (0.5 mark): The final mark was for calculating the corporation tax liability. This generally wasn’t a problem, although a few candidates kept the chargeable gain separate and then applied a different rate of tax on this. [Note that when this question was originally set there was only one rate of corporation tax and this calculation was for only half a mark.] As already mentioned, with computations containing both additions and deductions, candidates should be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions included as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. It is then just a matter of using the SUM function to get to a figure fo r taxable total profits. The simplicity of this approach is that the same layout can be used regardless of whether a profit or a loss is involved. The only aspects of the answer which warranted separate workings were the leasehold premium and the capital allowances. Everything else was easily dealt with within the main computation. Layout is not something candidates should really be concerned about on the day. With sufficient question practice, the correct layout becomes automatic. The only reason for giving more information (proceeds and expenditure) is so that the indexation allowance can be calculated. Where there are two or more gains, then each gain should be dealt with separately. This is a somewhat unusual presentation, although it is not dissimilar to that seen in a couple of other corporation tax questions. Here, however, the question is made slightly more difficult as it also involves reversing calculations which have already been done (incorrectly) to calculate correct figures. This question was not popular with students, many of whom did not know how to tackle it. It is important however, to attempt every question in the examination and therefore you should set out the computation, including the figures you do know, attempt the workings for those you don’t (making assumptions if necessary), and then go on to calculate the corporation tax liability, for which you will get follow through marks, even if parts of your answer are wrong. This part is also for 12 marks, and you must make sure you don’t overrun on time here. Part (b) requires you to identify why the company would not pay instalments in the current year and why they would be due in the following year. This should be straightforward provided these aspects of administration have been learnt. The highlighted words in the answer are key phrases that markers are looking for. --- PAGE 573 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE CORPORATION TAX QUESTIONS: SECTION 9 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 527 (a) Revised corporation tax computation – year ended 31 March 2026 Tutor’s top tips In a challenging question such as this, it is important to maximise marks with a systematic approach, making sure you score all the easy marks (of which there are many). Start by laying out your computation – inserting any obvious figures (e.g. figures provided in the question which you know are correct) and leaving blank the more difficult ones. Then work through the gaps, doing straightforward workings on the face of the computation and more detailed ones in referenced workings underneath. If you are not sure, make a decision and move on, do not waste time on one small point. For some figures, you need to reverse calculations which have been carried out incorrectly (some are not shown in the question), before doing revised calculations. This requires a good understanding of the way the calculations work, rather than just the ability to follow the pro forma and crunch the numbers. Tutorial note 1 The issue of preference shares is not a trading expense and therefore the associated legal fees are not an allowable deduction. 2 Legal fees are treated in the same way as the loan they relate to. No adjustment is therefore required. 7 Car 3 has CO 2 emissions over 50 grams per kilometre, and therefore only qualifies for writing down allowances at the rate of 6%. The extra 12% (18% – 6%) that had been calculated originally therefore needs to be deducted from the total capital allowances. 8 Car 4 has zero emissions, and therefore qualifies for 100% first year allowance. In the absence of any other information, assume that cars purchased are new (not second- hand). Therefore, an additional allowance of 82% (100% – 18%) needs to be included. 9 The scrapping of the computer equipment is a disposal for capital allowances purposes. The company should therefore have received a 100% balancing allowance rather than a writing down allowance at the rate of 18%. The 82/18 adjustment represents the additional 82% (100% – 18%) of the brought forward TWDV which can be deducted. This could also have been calculated by comparing the correct balancing allowance (£1,512/18% = £8,400) with the amount that had previously been deducted (£1,512). 10 As the repairs were carried out in order to make the warehouse usable, they are treated as capital in nature and are therefore disallowed. However, structures and buildings allowance (SBA) at 3% can be claimed on these costs since they were incurred after 1 April 2020 (the relevant date for TX exams). SBA can only be claimed from the date the property was brought into use, i.e. the day it was first let out – 1 July 2025. 11 Property and interest income must be dealt with on an accruals basis, therefore an adjustment is required for the rent due and the correct loan interest accrual. --- PAGE 575 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE CORPORATION TAX QUESTIONS: SECTION 9 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 529 (b) Quarterly instalment payments Tutor’s top tips Being able to determine when corporation tax is payable is a common examination requirement, and it is important to learn the rules about which companies must pay by quarterly instalments and the exceptions from that system, which are relevant here. • Large companies have to make quarterly instalment payments in respect of their corporation tax liability. A large comp any is one with augmented profits exceeding £1,500,000, adjusted for sh ort accounting periods and associated companies. • However, a company is not required to make quarterly instalment payments in the first year that it is large. Therefore, E-Commerce plc will not have been required to make instalment payments for the year ended 31 March 2026 as it was not a large company in the year ended 31 March 2025. This is because the augmented profits of £1,360,000 were less than £1,500,000. • For the year ended 31 March 2027, this exception will not apply. Therefore, E-Commerce plc will have to make quarterly instalment payments as its augmented profits will exceed £1,500,000. RELIEF FOR TRADING LOSSES 262 COP LTD Key answer tips This question requires the calculation of a company's taxable total profits for a three-month accounting period. It encompasses adjustments to trading profit, capital allowances, and the computation of a chargeable gain. You should begin by adjusting the given accounting loss for non-allowable expenses. Make sure you include a zero for the items where no adjustment is required as per the instructions in the question. When calculating capital allowances remember to think about the impact of the short accounting period on the different allowances. When calculating the chargeable gain on the investment property, ensure you include all incidental costs of acquisition and disposal. Apply indexation allowance to both the original cost and any enhancement expenditure up to December 2017. Finally, the trading loss should be offset against the total profits, and remember to deduct any qualifying charitable donations. --- PAGE 579 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE CORPORATION TAX QUESTIONS: SECTION 9 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 533 Taxable total profits for the three-month period ended 31 December 2025 £ Loss before taxation (13,000) Depreciation 45,000 Donations: Political party 250 Qualifying charitable donation 300 Legal and professional fees: Disposal of investment property 115,000 Bad debt recovery 0 Redundancy advice 0 Supplier contracts 0 Promotional gifts: Umbrellas 0 Biscuits 200 Briefcases 400 Annual party 0 Capital allowances (working 1) (293,455) ––––––– Trading loss (145,305) ––––––– Computation of taxable total profits £ Trading income 0 Chargeable gain (working 2) 1,297,340 –––––––– Total profits 1,297,340 Trading losses deducted from total profits (145,305) Qualifying charitable donation (300) –––––––– Taxable total profits 1,151,735 –––––––– Tutorial notes 1 The umbrellas cost less than £50 each and carry advertising so are an allowable expense. 2 The biscuits are food and so are not an allowable expense. 3 The briefcases cost more than £50 each and so are not an allowable expense. --- PAGE 580 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 534 KAPLAN PUBLISHING Working 1 – Capital allowances AIA Full expense Main pool Special rate pool Allowances £ £ £ £ £ TWDV brought forward 30,000 Additions not qual. for AIA: Car (1) 57,000 Additions qualifying for AIA: Machine 270,000 AIA (£1,000,000 × 3/12) (250,000) 250,000 ––––––– 20,000 Full expensing (100% FYA) (20,000) 20,000 –––––– Addition qualifying for FYA: Car (2) 22,000 FYA (22,000) 22,000 ––––––– Proceeds car (1) (50,000) –––––– –––––– 30,000 7,000 WDA – 18% × 3/12 (1,350) 1,350 WDA – 6% × 3/12 (105) 105 –––––– –––––– TWDV carried forward 28,650 6,895 –––––– –––––– ––––––– Total allowances 293,455 ––––––– Tutorial notes 1 Car (1) had CO 2 emissions over 50g/km and therefore qualifies for writing down allowances at 6%. The question required candidates to calculate Cop Ltd’s trading loss and taxable total profits for the three-month period 1 October to 31 December. As for the income tax question, there were various ways of approaching this question. Again, the easiest one was to have a main computation working out the trading loss, with this then extended to include the chargeable gain and qualifying charitable donation to arrive at a figure for taxable total profits. Capital allowances and the chargeable gain both warranted separate workings. In regard to the main computation, there were two issues which sometimes caused problems: • Candidates were instructed to indicate by the use of zero (0) any items which did not require adjustment. There were in fact five items of expenditure where no adjustment was required (because they were allowable), representing a total of 2.5 marks. A number of candidates did not do as instructed and therefore would not have gained these very easy 2.5 marks even if the remainder of their workings were correct. Remember it is important to read and follow the instructions given in the requirement. • With this type of answer containing both additions and deductions, candidates should be very careful to indicate which is which. A single column approach with deductions shown clearly as such on the spreadsheet avoids any confusion. Those candidates who did not show the deductions clearly invariably had problems when it came to showing totals with negative entries, and it was sometimes difficult for markers to determine whether a figure was a plus or a minus. One other point to bear in mind is that candidates should answer a question in the order in which information is provided. The information was provided in the order (1) donations, (2) legal and professional fees, (3) promotional costs and (4) annual party. So, adjustments should follow the same sequence. If this a pproach is followed, it allows markers the opportunity to sometimes award a mark where an obvious mistake has been made. Capital allowances The fact that the accounting period was only three months long meant care had to be taken with the capital allowances working: • The £1,000,000 annual investment allowance expenditure limit was £1,000,000 × 3/12 = £250,000. • There was no restriction in regard to first-year allowances. • The 18% and 6% writing down allowances were both restricted by 3/12ths. Despite these complications, quite a number of candidates correctly calculated the capital allowances figure for 5 marks, with many achieving 4 or 4.5 marks. The main problem was with the car in the specia l rate pool which was bought (for £57,000) and sold (for £50,000) during the accounting period. Despite this being the only asset in the special rate pool, there was not a balancing adjustment, but, instead, a writing down allowance calculated as normal. --- PAGE 583 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE CORPORATION TAX QUESTIONS: SECTION 9 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 537 Chargeable gain The chargeable gain was probably the most difficult aspect of this question, especially as two separate indexation allowance workings were necessary. • The incidental costs had to be picked up from the disallowance of legal and professional fees. This figure was then deducted from the disposal proceeds, so was not relevant when it came to the indexation allowance calculations. • One surprising mistake was sometimes the indexation allowances were calculated, but then only those figures deducted and not the cost and enhancement expenditure figures on which the indexation allowances were based. Candidates should particularly note that the annual exempt amount is NOT relevant to corporation tax. 263 WRETCHED LTD (ADAPTED) Walk in the footsteps of a top tutor Key answer tips The first mark available was in relation to company residence and was straightforward. This is regularly tested in the examination. Also, remember to time apportion allowances, except for the first year allowance, for a short accounting period. The calculation of property income is tested regularly. This should have been straightforward as it was a standard computation. Crumble Ltd had made a trading loss for the nine-month period ended 31 December 2025, but had other income for this period and had taxable total profits for the year ended 31 March 2025. Requirement (a) – 7 marks This requirement was not answered as well as may be expected, given it was a fairly straightforward loss adjustment scenario: • Several candidates failed to score very easy marks by not indicating the non-adjustable items with a zero, despite being instructed to do so. There were seven such items, so this basic mistake could have cost a potential 3.5 marks. • The deduction for interest payable was ignored by many candidates, despite the requirement specifically referring to this note in the question scenario. On the other hand, few of those candidates who did include an adjustment computed the correct figure. The interest figure included in the summarised income statement was £8,750. This figure related to the period 1 Marc h to 30 September 2025. A further three months of interest therefore had to be added (£5,000 × 3/6 = £2,500), making a total interest deduction of £8,750 + £2,500 = £11,250. • Some candidates attempted to rewrite the summarised statement of profit or loss in order to get to the tax adjusted trading loss. Apart from ignoring the instruction to commence with the operating loss figure, this approach was much more complicated; making it difficult to gain all the marks. • The requirement specifically instructed candidates to ignore the information given in respect of the property business income and the chargeable gain, yet several candidates did not comply with this and wasted quite a bit of their time. • The best approach to this requirement was a single-column list commencing with the operating loss as a negative figure and listing the items referred to in the relevant notes. Provided the interest was also included as a negative, it was then just a case of using the SUM function to get to the tax adjusted trading loss. The simplicity of this approach is that the same layout can be used regardless of whether a profit or a loss is involved. --- PAGE 590 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 544 KAPLAN PUBLISHING Requirement (b) – 4 marks There were many good answers for this requirement, with quite a few candidates achieving full marks. Candidates had to take account of the property business income, the chargeable gain and the qualifying charitable donation, and were instructed in the requirement to only take account of this information. However, a number of candidates included the trading loss or even the taxable total profits for the previous period. Again, in doing so they would have certainly wasted time. The most common problem was with the chargeable gain where figures were provided for both the original cost and for the indexed cost. Some candidates invariably deducted both figures, and this resulted in a capital loss rath er than a chargeable ga in. Once again, this shows why it is important to read the question and requirements as carefully as possible. Requirement (c)(i) – 1 mark The correct answer was by 31 December 2027, which is two years from the end of the loss- making period. There were few correct answers for this requi rement, with answers spread across a wide range of alternative dates. Requirement (c)(ii) – 3 marks Although there were some perfect answers to this requirement, overall, it was not particularly well answered. Many candidates ignored the current period loss relief claim, with others calculating the revised corporation tax liability for the ye ar ended 31 March 2025 rather than the corporation tax refund. The answer was simply the trading loss (calcula ted in part (a)), less the current year total profits (the property business profits and chargeable gain from part (b)) at 25%. Even if this approach was used, however, many candidates included the current year qualifying charitable donation, thereby missing out on a half mark. Quite a few candidates just stated that the co rporation tax originally paid would be fully refunded. Although a mark was given for this, candidates needed to go further to gain any additional marks. For example, if a candidate’s own-figure trading loss was greater than total profits in the year ended 31 March 2025 (so that a full refund was in fact the correct answer), a further half mark was given for an appropriate explanation. --- PAGE 591 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE CORPORATION TAX QUESTIONS: SECTION 9 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 545 265 MOONCAKE LTD (ADAPTED) Key answer tips This question is based on corporation tax and is split into three requirements. Candidates often ended up with a reasonably correct answer to part (c)(i), where loss relief was claimed, but spent a lot of time on irrelevant workings in reaching that point. One common problem seen in part (b) was the inability to deal with negatives. The requirement was to calculate Mooncake Ltd's tax adjusted trading loss, commencing with the operating loss figure of £93,820. This meant that the adjustments for non-allowable expenditure reduced the amount of loss, but the loss was increased by capital allowances. As shown in the suggested solution, the easies t approach was to start with £93,820 as a negative figure, show non-allowable expenditure as positive figures and then include capital allowances as another negative. This is then consistent with a profit adjustment question commencing with a profit, avoiding the loss of some easy marks if negatives and positives are confused. The total can then be obtained using the SUM function on the spreadsheet. Some candidates showed all figures as positive and then tried to calculate the total within the cell on the lines of – A1+A2+A3-A4. It is also very easy to make mistakes using this approach. The only aspect requiring a separate working was one for capital allowances. Requirement (a) Although many candidates easily picked up the [three] available marks, many instead wrote at length about available loss reliefs. The fact that this requirement is just for [3] marks, together with the use of ‘state’ should be a very good indication that only a short set of answers is required. This is why it is important to make use of the model answers since candidates’ answers should, ideally, not be any longer than those. Candidates who mentioned loss of personal allowances or annual exempt amounts had, worryingly, confused income and corporation taxes. Requirement (b) When answering this type of question, candidates are advised to answer in the same order as information is presented. So here, the first item was depreciation, and that, therefore, should have been the first adjustment. This approach makes it easier for markers to follow a candidate’s answer, and there is less scope for missing out any of the adjustments. As can be seen from the suggested solution, the capital allowances working was fairly straightforward, involving just a main pool. There were three disposal figures to deduct from the brought forward written down value, with an 18% writing down allowance calculated on the remaining balance. The only reason for pr oviding the cost figures was so that (where relevant) proceeds could be restricted to original cost. However, many candidates included the cost figures as additions, and there were then various permutations involving balancing adjustments. Again, this is why question practice is so important. It should also be noted that none of the other information (property business loss and profit on disposal of shares) was relevant to this part of the question since the requirement was just to calculate the tax adjusted trading loss. --- PAGE 595 --- ANSWERS TO PRACTICE CORPORATION TAX QUESTIONS: SECTION 9 KAPLAN PUBLISHING 549 Requirement (c)(i) With only losses for the year ended 31 March 2026, there was obviously no income. However, this should have been indicated by the use of zeros (0). There was no chargeable gain because the indexation allowance of £6,700 exceeded the gain of £3,700. This did not create a loss, and there was no need to utilise the capital loss brought forward from the year ended 31 March 2025. These were both common mistakes made by candidates. Another common mistake was to carry back the property business loss. Many candidates assumed that the qualifying charitable donations for the year ended 31 March 2025 were wasted despite the trading loss being considerably less than income. The suggested solution shows how it is much easier to lay out this type of answer using a two-column approach with one column for each year. Although most candi dates did reasonably well in this part, there were not many perfect answers. Requirement (c)(ii) Although marks were awarded based on what candidates had done in part (c)(i), the need to carry out an overall review and see what was left appeared to be challenging for many candidates. The correct answer was that there was an unused capital loss from the year ended 31 March 2025, and a property business loss from the year ended 31 March 2026. For full marks, it was also necessary to show that the trading loss had been fully utilised, and that the unused qualifying charitable donations from the year ended 31 March 2026 were wasted. So four points for a half-mark each, and what should have been a very short answer. There were very few perfect answers, with many candidates picking up just one or two half- marks and wasting time on unnecessary detailed workings. The use of ‘calculate’ in the requirement should have indicated that no explanation was necessary. WITH GROUP ASPECTS 266 MUSIC PLC (ADAPTED) Key answer tips In this question there are ten marks for written explanations of the gains group and associated company rules. It is important to st ate the basic rule and then apply to the facts of the question. Be careful with the overseas company, which is included but unable to enjoy the benefits of gains group status. The highlighted words in the answer are key phrases that markers are looking for. --- PAGE 596 --- TX–UK: TAXATION (FA2025) 550 KAPLAN PUBLISHING (a) Capital gains group • Companies form a capital gains group if at each level in the group structure there is a 75% shareholding, provided the parent company has an effective interest of more than 50%. • Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo Inc and Flute Ltd are all 75% subsidiaries, and Music plc has an effective interest of 60% (80% × 75%) in Flute Ltd. All of these companies therefore form a capital gains group. • However, Bass Ltd and Cello Ltd will only be included in respect of assets acquired or disposed of whilst they were members of the group. • Drum Ltd and Gong Ltd are not included as Drum Ltd is not a 75% subsidiary, and Music plc’s effective interest in Gong Ltd is only 48% (80% × 75% × 80%). • Although Echo Inc is included in the definition of the capital gains group, companies that are resident overseas are not able to take advantage of the provisions applicable to a capital gains group. (b) Associated companies • Alto Ltd, Bass Ltd, Cello Ltd, Echo In c, Flute Ltd and Gong Ltd are all under the common control of Music plc, and are therefore associated companies. • Companies associated for part of the accounting period, such as Bass Ltd and Cello Ltd, count as associated companies for the whole of the period. • For these purposes, it does not matter where a company is resident. Echo Inc is therefore included despite being resident overseas. • Drum Ltd is not included as an associated company since Music plc’s effective interest in this company is only 45%. This section was quite well answered. If asked to identify a company’s accounting periods throughout a given period candidates should make sure that all relevant periods are stated. It does not create a good impression if there are gaps between the accounting periods stated by a candidate, or if a stated period ends before it has started. Part (a)(ii) required candidates to explain Ash Ltd’s residence status throughout the same period. There was a rights issue which had taken place in the month of purchase, so there was no need to index prior to adding the new shares into the share pool. Part 92: Professional Ethics Master: Evasion vs Avoidance, GAAR & MLR

Professional Conduct in Relation to Taxation (PCRT), General Anti-Abuse Rule (GAAR), Money Laundering Regulations (MLR), and disclosure duties.

⚖️ Ethics Framework Summary

1. Evasion: Illegal suppression or misrepresentation of tax facts (Criminal offense).

2. Avoidance: Legal arrangement of tax affairs within the law (Subject to GAAR counteraction if abusive).

3. Money Laundering Duties: Disclose suspicious transactions to MLRO/NCA. Tipping off client is a criminal offense!

Part 93: Official ACCA Specimen Exam — Section A OTQs (Q1–Q15)

Official specimen 30-mark Section A test with detailed answer keys and workings.

Specimen Q1 • William's Class 4 NIC
+10 XP Specimen OTQ

William is self-employed (trading profit £82,700 in 2025/26). Paid £5,400 (gross) into personal pension. What Class 4 NIC will William pay?

Trading Profit: £82,700 Note: Pension contributions DO NOT reduce trading profit for Class 4 NIC purposes! Class 4 NIC Band 1 (£12,571 to £50,270): (£50,270 - £12,570) = £37,700 × 6% = £2,262 Class 4 NIC Band 2 (Over £50,270): (£82,700 - £50,270) = £32,430 × 2% = £648.60 Total Class 4 NIC = £2,262 + £648.60 = £2,910.60 -> £2,911
CORRECT ANSWER: B (£2,911)
Personal pension contributions extend income tax bands but have NO EFFECT on Class 4 NIC calculations!

Specimen Q33 • Corporation Tax Constructed Response (15 Marks)
+40 XP Specimen Masterclass
Specimen Corporation Tax Computation (12-Month AP): Trading Profit: £420,000 Property Business Income: £18,000 Chargeable Gain: £32,000 -------- Net Total Profits: £470,000 Less Qualifying Charitable Donations (QCD): (£5,000) -------- Taxable Total Profits (TTP): £465,000 Corporation Tax Rate Check: Augmented Profits (£465k + £0 exempt dividends) = £465,000 Upper Limit £250,000 (No associated companies) -> TTP > £250,000. Taxed at MAIN RATE 25%! Corporation Tax Liability = £465,000 × 25% = £116,250
🔴 OFFICIAL TUTOR DEBRIEF
"Where Augmented Profits exceed £250,000, the company pays Corporation Tax at the Main Rate of 25% without Marginal Relief. Ensure QCDs are deducted from Total Profits AFTER property income and gains are added!"

Part 99: Appendix B — Time Limits, Election Dates & 50 Deadly Traps

Statutory claims limits and the top 50 candidate mistakes flagged by examiners.

⚠️ Top 10 High-Frequency Exam Traps

  1. Forgetting to taper Personal Allowance when ANI exceeds £100,000.
  2. Applying Full Expensing (100% FYA) to sole traders (applies ONLY to companies!).
  3. Including pension contributions when calculating Class 4 NICs (they do not reduce NIC).
  4. Claiming AIA on motor cars (cars are EXCLUDED from AIA).
  5. Applying 4% diesel surcharge to RDE2 compliant diesel cars.
  6. Reducing car benefits for partial business use (business use % is IGNORED).
  7. Dividing CT upper/lower limits by associated companies including dormant companies (dormants are EXCLUDED).
  8. Applying CGT AEA (£3,000) against BADR gains (14%) instead of higher rate gains (24%).
  9. Applying IHT taper relief to the gift value instead of the tax payable.
  10. Forgetting 60-day deadline for UK residential property CGT returns and payments.
🔴 EXAMINER REPORT — 50 Deadly Traps — Summary (p.280–294)

Key examiner-confirmed traps: PA taper (ANI>£100k), no Full Expensing for sole traders, AIA excludes cars, RDE2 diesel exempt from 4%, IHT taper on tax not gift value, 60-day CGT property deadline.

📋 BATCH EXAMINER FEEDBACK — Part 99 (Traps — PA taper / Full Expensing sole traders / AIA cars / Diesel / 60-day / IHT taper) — PDF VERIFIED

Examiner reports (p.260 / p.266 / p.273 / p.280–294) confirm: Always check PA taper (>£100k ANI), exclude dormant associates, use 3/200 marginal fraction, apply AEA to higher-rate gains first, and verify 60-day property deadline.

Common trap: Forgetting transferable PA requires neither spouse at higher/additional rate; joint property election may increase liability.

⚠️ 50 DEADLY TRAPS — Click to Reveal

These are the most common mistakes flagged by ACCA examiners. Click each one to reveal the answer.

1. PA taper when ANI > £100,000?
✓ YES — PA reduced by £1 per £2 above £100k. Zero PA at £125,140.
2. Full Expensing for sole traders?
✗ NO — Full Expensing (100% FYA) applies ONLY to companies. Sole traders use AIA.
3. Pension reduces Class 4 NIC?
✗ NO — Pension contributions extend IT bands but have NO effect on NIC.
4. AIA on motor cars?
✗ NO — Cars are EXCLUDED from AIA. They go into main/special rate pool only.
5. 4% diesel surcharge for RDE2?
✗ NO — RDE2-compliant diesels are EXEMPT from the 4% surcharge.
6. Business use reduces car benefit?
✗ NO — Car benefit is NOT reduced for business use. Private use % is irrelevant.
7. Dormant companies count as associated?
✗ NO — Dormant companies are EXCLUDED from the associated company count.
8. Apply AEA against BADR gains first?
✗ NO — Apply AEA against higher-rate gains (24%) first to maximise tax saving!
9. IHT taper relief reduces gift value?
✗ NO — Taper relief reduces the TAX PAYABLE, not the gift value!
10. 60-day CGT property deadline?
✓ YES — 60 days from completion for UK residential property CGT return AND payment.
